articles.title: Your 100% Lighthouse A11y Score Is a Lie: The Visual Architecture Guide to the Browser Accessibility Tree
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into web accessibility architecture. Learn how browsers construct the Accessibility Tree from the DOM, why custom ARIA divs create more errors than native HTML, how CSS visibility properties alter screen reader output, and how to build leak-free accessible focus traps.
articles.body_html:
You open Chrome DevTools. You navigate to the Lighthouse tab, click "Analyze page load," and wait thirty seconds while the audit completes.

The circular gauge spins, stops, and turns bright emerald green:

Accessibility: 100 / 100

You smile, push your code to production, and congratulate yourself on shipping an inclusive, accessible web application.

Then an actual screen reader user visits your website.

They press the Tab key to navigate your navigation menu, and the focus ring vanishes into thin air. They trigger a modal window to update their billing address, but the screen reader continues reading paragraphs hidden underneath the backdrop. They fill out a form, click your custom button, and hear nothing:

"Button. Unlabelled. Clickable."

When an error banner appears, the screen reader remains completely silent. The user has no idea whether their payment succeeded, failed, or timed out. Frustrated and disoriented, they abandon your application.

How could a website with a perfect 100% Lighthouse accessibility score be virtually unusable for someone relying on assistive technology?

Because automated accessibility audits only check static, programmatic rules: whether images have alt tags, whether color contrast meets basic thresholds, and whether input fields have matching labels.

Automated scanners catch roughly 30% to 40% of web accessibility barriers. They cannot test whether your keyboard tab order makes logical sense. They cannot verify whether your custom modal traps focus. And they cannot tell you if your ARIA attributes are actively breaking the browser's internal accessibility tree.

In fact, the annual WebAIM Million audit of the top one million websites repeatedly uncovers a staggering paradox: pages with ARIA attributes present an average of 41% more accessibility errors than pages without ARIA.

To build digital products that work for everyone, you must understand how assistive technology actually experiences your code: the Accessibility Tree, the First Rule of ARIA, CSS visibility traps, and focus management.

Here is the architectural reality of web accessibility.

1. The Dual-Tree Architecture: How Browsers Construct the Accessibility Tree

When a web developer thinks about a web page, they visualize the DOM (Document Object Model): a tree of HTML nodes that JavaScript inspects and modifies.

When the browser renders that page, it constructs a CSSOM (CSS Object Model), merges it with the DOM, and produces the Render Tree to paint pixels on your display.

However, screen readers (like VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, NVDA and JAWS on Windows, and TalkBack on Android) do not read your DOM, and they do not inspect your Render Tree.

Instead, the browser constructs a parallel, internal data structure: the Accessibility Tree (Accessibility Object Model / AOM).

The Anatomy of an Accessibility Node

Every node in the Accessibility Tree contains four fundamental attributes computed by the browser:

  1. Role: What the element is (e.g., button, heading, checkbox, dialog, link).
  2. Name: The human-readable label of the element (e.g., "Submit payment", "Close window").
  3. State: The current condition of the widget (e.g., focused, expanded: true, checked: false, disabled).
  4. Value: The current numerical or textual value (e.g., "50%", "John Doe").

How the Browser Communicates with the Operating System

The browser does not talk directly to screen reader software.

Instead, the browser translates the Accessibility Tree into platform-specific native operating system accessibility APIs:

  • Windows: UIAutomation, IAccessible2, MSAA
  • macOS / iOS: NSAccessibility, UIAccessibility
  • Linux: AT-SPI (Assistive Technology Service Provider Interface)

When a blind user presses the Tab key, their screen reader queries the operating system's accessibility API. The OS queries the browser's Accessibility Tree. The browser reports:
"Focused element is a Button, Name is 'Download Invoice', State is Enabled."

The screen reader synthesizes speech from that exact data. If an element does not exist in the Accessibility Tree, or if its role and name are garbled, it does not exist for the user.

2. The First Rule of ARIA: Why Your Custom Div Buttons Are Broken

ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It is a W3C specification designed to supplement HTML when native elements cannot express complex dynamic behavior.

However, the official W3C specification opens with a principle so critical that the authors codified it as The First Rule of ARIA:

"If you can use a native HTML element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, then do so instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible."

Why did the specification authors write this?

Because developers routinely write code like this:

<!-- DANGEROUS: The fake button anti-pattern -->
<div class="btn" role="button" onclick="handleSubmit()">
  Submit Order
</div>

A developer looks at this div, applies CSS to make it look like a button, adds role="button", and assumes they are done.

Lighthouse inspects the code, sees role="button" and readable text, and awards a green checkmark.

In reality, this fake button is completely broken.

The 6 Hidden Superpowers of a Native <button>

When you use a real HTML <button>, the browser provides six complex behaviors for free:

  1. Keyboard Focus: It is automatically included in the keyboard tab order without needing tabindex="0".
  2. Dual Key Activation: It fires click events on both the Enter key and the Space key.
  3. Space Key Scrolling Suppression: Pressing Space on a native button triggers the action without scrolling the entire web page down.
  4. Native Disabled State: Setting disabled automatically removes the button from the tab order and prevents click handlers from firing.
  5. Form Integration: Pressing Enter inside an input automatically submits the associated form through the button.
  6. OS High Contrast Support: The browser automatically renders high-contrast borders in Windows High Contrast Mode.

Rebuilding a Button from Scratch

If you insist on using <div role="button">, you must manually implement all six behaviors in JavaScript:

// Rebuilding what the browser gives you for free
const fakeButton = document.querySelector('.btn');

// 1. Make it focusable
fakeButton.setAttribute('tabindex', '0');

// 2. Listen for keyboard triggers
fakeButton.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  if (event.key === 'Enter' || event.key === ' ') {
    event.preventDefault(); // Stop spacebar scrolling
    handleSubmit();
  }
});

// 3. Handle disabled state manually
if (isDisabled) {
  fakeButton.setAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true');
  fakeButton.removeAttribute('tabindex');
}

You just wrote twenty lines of fragile, bug-prone JavaScript to recreate what <button>Submit Order</button> does in zero lines of code.

No ARIA is better than bad ARIA. Always prefer semantic HTML.

3. The CSS Visibility Trap: How Styles Alter the Accessibility Tree

Most frontend developers believe CSS only controls visual layout on screen.

In modern browsers, CSS properties directly alter the Accessibility Tree.

Choosing the wrong hiding technique creates invisible ghost elements that trap keyboard users, or accidentally silences screen readers when elements are supposed to be heard.

Case 1: display: none and visibility: hidden

When you apply display: none or visibility: hidden:

  • The element is completely removed from the visual Render Tree.
  • The element is completely removed from the Accessibility Tree.
  • Screen readers will never announce it, and keyboard users cannot tab to it.

This is the correct choice when content should be completely hidden from all users (such as an unexpanded accordion panel or a closed dropdown menu).

Case 2: opacity: 0 (The Ghost Tab Trap)

When an element has opacity: 0:

  • It is completely invisible on the visual screen.
  • It remains 100% active in the Accessibility Tree.
  • It remains fully focusable by the Tab key!

If you animate a mobile navigation drawer off-screen using opacity: 0 without setting visibility: hidden or display: none, keyboard users will tab through ten invisible menu links floating in empty space.

Case 3: The Visually Hidden Pattern (.sr-only)

What if you have an icon button (like a shopping cart or search magnifying glass) that visual users understand through iconography, but screen reader users need descriptive text for?

Do not use opacity: 0. Use the standardized .sr-only (screen-reader only) CSS utility:

.sr-only {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
  padding: 0;
  margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip-path: inset(50%);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border: 0;
}

<button class="cart-btn">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" class="icon-cart"></svg>
  <span class="sr-only">View shopping cart (3 items)</span>
</button>

How this works:

  1. aria-hidden="true" removes the purely decorative SVG from the Accessibility Tree, preventing screen readers from announcing "graphic, path, vector".
  2. The .sr-only span shrinks to a 1-pixel clipped box that is invisible to the eye.
  3. The browser keeps the text inside the Accessibility Tree, so VoiceOver reads: "View shopping cart (3 items), button".

Case 4: The :focus-visible Revolution

For over a decade, frontend developers committed the ultimate accessibility crime:

/* NEVER DO THIS */
*:focus {
  outline: none;
}

Designers complained that clicking a button with a mouse created an ugly blue outline, so developers erased the focus ring entirely.

In doing so, they blinded millions of keyboard users who navigate using Tab and depend on that focus ring to know where they are on the page.

Modern CSS solved this conflict with the :focus-visible pseudo-class:

/* Remove outline ONLY for mouse clicks, preserve it for keyboard navigation */
button:focus {
  outline: none;
}

button:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid #38BDF8;
  outline-offset: 4px;
}

:focus-visible only renders when the browser detects keyboard navigation or assistive device input. Mouse clicks stay clean, while keyboard users receive a crisp, high-contrast navigation ring.

4. Focus Architecture: Building Accessible Modals and Dialogs

Modals and dialogs are the single most common source of critical accessibility failures in modern web applications.

When an inaccessible modal opens:

  1. The user clicks "Edit Profile".
  2. The modal appears visually on screen.
  3. Keyboard focus remains stuck on the background page.
  4. Pressing Tab moves focus behind the dark modal backdrop, clicking unseen links and triggering unintended actions.
  5. Pressing Escape does nothing.
  6. Closing the modal causes focus to reset to the top of the <body>, forcing the user to tab through the entire navigation bar again.

An accessible modal requires a strict four-step lifecycle:

Step 1: Semantic Markup and ARIA Attributes

Your modal container must inform assistive technology that it is an isolated dialog:

<div 
  id="edit-modal" 
  role="dialog" 
  aria-modal="true" 
  aria-labelledby="modal-title"
  class="modal"
>
  <h2 id="modal-title">Edit Your Profile</h2>
  <!-- Form fields -->
  <button id="close-btn">Close</button>
</div>
  • role="dialog" announces to screen readers that an interactive dialog has opened.
  • aria-modal="true" instructs assistive technologies to treat the dialog as modal, ignoring elements outside it.
  • aria-labelledby="modal-title" automatically reads the heading when the modal opens.

Step 2: Focus Trapping

Focus must never escape the bounds of the active dialog:

  • When focus is on the last interactive element (e.g., the "Save" button) and the user presses Tab, focus must wrap back to the first interactive element (e.g., the "Close" button).
  • When focus is on the first element and the user presses Shift + Tab, focus must wrap to the last element.

Step 3: The Native inert Breakthrough

Historically, trapping focus required complex JavaScript listeners counting DOM elements.

Today, modern browsers support the native HTML inert attribute:

// Opening the modal
const mainContent = document.querySelector('#app-content');
const modal = document.querySelector('#edit-modal');

// Make the entire background page inert in one line!
mainContent.setAttribute('inert', '');
modal.classList.add('is-open');

When an element is marked inert, the browser automatically:

  1. Prevents all pointer and click events on background nodes.
  2. Removes all background elements from the keyboard tab order.
  3. Removes all background elements from the Accessibility Tree.

Step 4: Deterministic Focus Restoration

When the user closes the modal (either by clicking Close or pressing the Escape key):

// Remember the button that triggered the modal
let previousActiveElement = null;

function openModal(triggerElement) {
  previousActiveElement = triggerElement;
  modal.show();
  modal.querySelector('input').focus();
}

function closeModal() {
  modal.hide();
  mainContent.removeAttribute('inert');

  // Return focus back to where the user started!
  if (previousActiveElement) {
    previousActiveElement.focus();
  }
}

Restoring focus guarantees that keyboard users can resume navigating immediately without losing their place on the page.

5. Dynamic Real-Time Announcements: Mastering Live Regions (aria-live)

In traditional multi-page websites, submitting a form refreshed the entire browser tab. The screen reader detected a page load, moved to the top of the new document, and announced the heading.

In modern Single Page Applications (React, Vue, Svelte, Next.js), state updates occur asynchronously without page refreshes.

When a user clicks "Add to Cart":

  • A microtask runs.
  • A green toast notification appears in the bottom right corner: "Item added to cart."
  • A visual user sees the toast instantly.

To a screen reader user, absolutely nothing happened.

Unless you explicitly inform the browser, the Accessibility Tree does not announce dynamic visual changes.

The Solution: Live Regions

An ARIA Live Region is a DOM node designated to monitor content changes and announce them via assistive technology:

<!-- A polite notification container -->
<div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" class="sr-only toast-announcer" id="live-region">
  <!-- Dynamic messages injected here -->
</div>

The Difference Between polite and assertive

  • aria-live="polite": The screen reader waits until the user finishes their current sentence or action before reading the update. Use this for 95% of notifications (e.g., cart updates, form saved confirmations, search result counts).
  • aria-live="assertive": The screen reader immediately interrupts whatever it is currently saying to announce the message. Reserve this strictly for critical, time-sensitive emergencies (e.g., session timeout warnings, server connection lost, validation errors blocking submission).

The Golden Rule of Live Regions

The live region container must already exist in the DOM when the page loads.

If you dynamically create a <div aria-live="polite"> in JavaScript and immediately populate it with text, the browser will not register the live region in time to announce it.

Always render an empty live container in your root layout and update its textContent when events fire:

function announceToScreenReader(message) {
  const liveRegion = document.getElementById('live-region');
  liveRegion.textContent = ''; // Clear previous message
  setTimeout(() => {
    liveRegion.textContent = message; // Triggers fresh OS announcement
  }, 50);
}

6. The 5-Step Developer Accessibility Audit

You do not need an expensive third-party consultancy to ensure your web application is accessible.

Before opening a pull request, run this 5-minute manual engineering checklist:

Step 1: The No-Mouse Challenge (Keyboard Navigation)

Unplug your mouse or turn off your trackpad. Navigate your entire user flow using only Tab, Shift + Tab, Enter, Space, and Escape:

  • Can you see where the focus ring is at all times?
  • Can you reach every button, link, and input?
  • Do custom dropdowns open and close with the keyboard?
  • Does pressing Escape close modals and menus?

Step 2: The Screen Reader Dry Run

Turn on your operating system's built-in screen reader (press Cmd + F5 for VoiceOver on macOS, or Win + Ctrl + Enter for Narrator on Windows).
Close your eyes and try to complete the core user task (e.g., sign up, search, add an item to cart). Listen to the announcements. Are buttons labelled properly, or do you hear "clickable, unlabelled"?

Step 3: Zoom and Reflow Testing

Press Cmd + Plus (or Ctrl + Plus) until your browser zoom reaches 200%:

  • Does your layout break into overlapping text?
  • Does content get cut off inside fixed-height containers?
  • Does horizontal scrolling appear unnecessarily?

Step 4: Color and Contrast Verification

Use Chrome DevTools to inspect your text elements. Ensure standard text achieves at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its background (3:1 for large 18pt+ headings). Never convey information through color alone (e.g., don't just turn an input border red on error; include an error text message and an icon).

Step 5: Inspect the Accessibility Tree

Open Chrome DevTools, click the Elements tab, and switch to the Accessibility sub-tab. Click any interactive widget on your page. Look at the computed Name and Role. If the computed name is empty or incorrect, fix your HTML semantics immediately.

The Mental Shift

Web accessibility is not an extra feature you bolt onto a web application during the final sprint before release.

Accessibility is fundamental web engineering quality.

  • Semantic HTML gives you keyboard support, focusability, and OS integrations for free.
  • ARIA is not a styling tool; it is a communication protocol with assistive technology.
  • The browser constructs an Accessibility Tree alongside your visual layout, and both trees must be maintained with equal engineering rigor.

When you stop treating accessibility as an afterthought and start respecting the browser's dual-tree architecture, your Lighthouse scores stay high, your code stays lean, and your digital products become usable for every human being on the internet.

How does your team handle accessibility audits and testing in your CI/CD pipelines? Have you encountered surprising bugs when inspecting the browser Accessibility Tree, or experienced the ARIA paradox in production? Share your thoughts and testing strategies in the comments below.

articles.title: Five Palaces, One Model: Testing Google’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen in AI Studio
articles.description: Last week Google shipped Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and within hours my X timeline was nothing but 3D scenes,...
articles.body_html:
Last week Google shipped Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and within hours my X timeline was nothing but 3D scenes, animations and generative art built from a single prompt. I couldn't just scroll past it, so I opened a browser tab and started building.

The result is Imperial Palaces: an interactive 3D world with five hand-coded (well, Hydrogen-coded) palaces, five camera views, a golden-hour/moonlit lighting switch, falling petals you can turn up to a blizzard, a synthesized koto soundtrack, and a one-click PNG snapshot.

👉 Live demo: palaces-eight.vercel.app
👉 Source: github.com/amananandrai/Palaces

What is Gemini 4 Hydrogen?

Quick context if you missed the launch. Hydrogen is the fast, cheaper tier of the Gemini 4 family. It sits next to the heavier Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon models and replaces the old "Flash" branding.

  • Launched: November 12, 2026
  • Built for: everyday coding and agentic workflows
  • Speed: Google says it finishes tasks about 2.5× faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash
  • Context: 1M-token context window, with four thinking levels (low, medium, high (the default) and a new xhigh)
  • Where to use it: Gemini app, Google Search, Google AI Studio, the Gemini API and Antigravity
  • API pricing: $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens

Here's the official announcement:

The inspiration: X went wild

What got me to open AI Studio wasn't the benchmark chart. It was the stuff people were making.

A code-based painting. Vamsi Batchu shared artwork that looks hand-painted but is pure single-file code: no external libraries, no image generators and no embedded assets. He gave Hydrogen a reference image and asked for a range of subjects in that painterly, gouache-like style.

Hydrogen vs. 3.8 Flash on the same 3D scene. Google itself boosted this one: the same animated 3D desert ranch prompt run on both models, with Hydrogen bringing the scene to life in under a minute.

A 3D city on an open book. This one came from before launch, while Hydrogen was being tested anonymously on Arena. Pankaj Kumar asked it for a 3D city sitting on an open book, and the whole site was generated in under 4 minutes.

And if you want the full firehose, Min Choi's roundup threads are a great rabbit hole:

Attempt #1: the Gemini app (didn't go well)

My first move was the obvious one: open the Gemini app and describe the scene I wanted, a Japanese Edo-era castle in a sakura garden.

The results weren't close to what I was seeing on X. The scenes were flatter and less detailed, and iterating on them felt clunky. Part of the reason is that free users in the Gemini app get Hydrogen through automatic model selection, so you don't always know which model is answering. The app is also built for chat, not for iterating on a multi-file 3D project.

Attempt #2: Google AI Studio (this is where it clicked)

So I moved to Google AI Studio, picked Gemini 4 Hydrogen explicitly, and used its app-building mode. That changed everything:

  • I knew exactly which model and thinking level I was using.
  • The output was a real React + TypeScript + Three.js + Vite project, not a single blob of HTML.
  • I could preview it live and keep refining in place.

From one castle to five palaces

The first good version was just the Edo Sanctuary: a multi-tiered castle keep, cherry trees, an arched red taiko-bashi bridge over a stream, stone lanterns, a koi pond and a sunset mountain backdrop. From there I refined it over a few rounds:

  1. Camera presets. Instead of only free-orbiting, I asked for curated views that fly the camera smoothly to the pond, the bridge, the palace and the horizon.
  2. Time of day. A Golden Hour / Moonlit Night toggle that blends the sun, sky, hemisphere light and water reflections instead of hard-cutting.
  3. Atmosphere controls. Calm / Breeze / Flurry petal density (240 → 640 → 1,200 particles) plus a wind-strength slider.
  4. Sound. An ambient soundscape made entirely with the Web Audio API.
  5. Snapshot. Export the current view as a PNG.
  6. More palaces. Russian, Victorian, Mughal and Persian scenes, each with its own bridge, water feature and particle type.

By the end the project was roughly 12,000 lines of TypeScript, and the codebase has no image or audio files to speak of: textures, geometry and sound are all generated in code.

The tour

Five camera views

The dock at the bottom has five presets. Pick one and the camera glides there; drag the scene and you're back to free orbit.

Grand Vista: the establishing shot shown at the top of this post.

Pond View: koi swimming under lily pads, with a wooden viewing pier in the corner.

Bridge View: the red taiko-bashi bridge over the stream.

Palace View: up close with the castle keep's tiered roofs and gold crests.

Horizon View: pulled back toward the mountains and the setting sun.

Breeze: petals and wind

Petal density has three levels, Calm, Breeze (the default) and Flurry, and the wind slider controls how hard the petals drift. Here it is on Flurry:

The particle type changes with each palace: sakura petals in Japan, snowfall in Russia, twilight motes at the Victorian manor and blossom or desert breezes in the Mughal and Persian scenes.

Moonlit Night

One click turns golden hour into a moonlit night. The sky goes deep indigo, the stars come out, the lanterns and windows glow warm, and the moon leaves a streak of light on the pond.

The pond at night is my favorite spot in the whole project:

Snapshot

The Snapshot button in the top right grabs the WebGL canvas with canvas.toDataURL('image/png') and downloads it as palace-<style>-<timeOfDay>.png. This is an untouched export straight from the button:

Five palaces

The top nav switches between five architectural styles, and each comes with its own setting:

Russian: Winter Terem Kremlin. Onion domes, a frozen rink, ice fishing, snowy pines and a granite bridge.

Victorian: Gothic Tudor Manor. A clock tower, a cast-iron arch bridge and a swan fountain lake.

Mughal: Diwan-i-Khas. White domes and chhatris, a stone bridge and an octagonal charbagh pool.

Persian: Safavid Desert Oasis. Turquoise tile domes, a triple-arch bridge, a qanat lagoon and palms.

Zen mode

Press H (or "Hide Controls") to slide the dock away and just enjoy the view.

Under the hood

A few things in the generated code impressed me:

  • Procedural textures. Stone, roof tiles, plaster, the namako lattice walls and hinoki wood are all painted at runtime onto CanvasTextures, with matching bump maps.
  • Instanced foliage. Blossoms, leaves, grass blades and cattails use THREE.InstancedMesh with per-instance colors, so thousands of petals stay smooth.
  • Synthesized audio. The ambient engine builds stream water and garden wind from filtered noise, and plays koto-style plucks on a D Hirajoshi pentatonic scale. There isn't a single audio file in it.
  • Smooth transitions. Camera presets and the day/night blend are lerped inside the render loop through refs, so React doesn't re-render every frame.

Stack: React 19 · TypeScript · Three.js · Vite · Tailwind CSS · lucide-react · deployed on Vercel.

What I learned

  1. The tool matters as much as the model. The same model gave me mediocre results in the chat app and great ones in AI Studio. Choosing the model explicitly and getting a real project structure made all the difference.
  2. Get a good v1, then iterate. Hydrogen is fast enough that "make the water reflect the moon" or "add four more palaces" turns into a quick loop instead of a big ask.
  3. The demos on X are real. I went in skeptical and came out with something I'm happy to share.

Go try it, flip to Moonlit Night, crank the petals to Flurry and take a snapshot:

🏯 palaces-eight.vercel.app

If you build something with Hydrogen, drop it in the comments. I'd love to see it! ⭐ The repo is here if you want to poke at the code.

articles.title: A Third-Party Script Can Rewrite Your Deposit Address
articles.description: On November 16, people who visited Ledger's website could copy a crypto address from the page and...
articles.body_html:
On November 16, people who visited Ledger's website could copy a crypto address from the page and paste someone else's. Ledger's servers weren't breached. Neither were the servers of HSBC, the BBC, Salesforce, Zoom or IKEA, which had the same problem that day. The code came from Optimizely, the A/B testing tool all of them load on their pages.

I write a lot here about what crypto apps should check before a user presses "Send". This incident is a good reminder that the page itself can be the weak point, even when your own code is fine. If you build anything that shows a wallet address, a payment form or a withdrawal screen, it's worth going through what happened and what it changes.

How Optimizely runs on a page

Optimizely Web Experimentation works the way most A/B testing tools do. You add one script tag to your site, and that snippet loads on every page. Marketing teams then change headlines, layouts and copy from the Optimizely dashboard without touching the codebase.

Two details matter here:

  1. The snippet is served from Optimizely's infrastructure, not from your servers.
  2. Projects have an optional field for custom JavaScript. Whatever goes into that field runs in every visitor's browser, with the same access to the page as your own code.

That's the feature that makes these tools useful. It's also why a compromised vendor account is as good as a compromised website.

What happened on November 16

According to Optimizely, an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow. That gave them access to customer projects, and they added malicious code to the custom code field. Visitors' browsers then loaded it from a domain those sites already trusted (Bitcoin.com, CoinDesk).

Scott Helme of Report URI, a service that monitors scripts running on websites, checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets and found 188 infected ones across 178 organizations. The names in the reports include Ledger, HSBC, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, Zoom, GitLab, IKEA, Equifax and Air France-KLM. CoinDesk counted six crypto or trading businesses among them (Ledger, IG Group, OANDA's Coinpass, Interactive Investor, TMS Brokers and Betashares) and about 32 banks and financial companies.

The payload wasn't a single trick. It was a kit:

  • Address swapping. It looked for crypto addresses in form fields and in copied text and replaced them with the attacker's.
  • Card skimming. It captured card numbers typed into payment forms.
  • Session theft. It copied cookies and took screenshots.
  • Device attacks. It served exploit kits to older iPhones and iPads.

Timeline (UTC)

The rough sequence, pieced together from Bitcoin.com and Shattered.io's summary of StepSecurity's analysis. Some timestamps come from secondary reporting, so treat them as approximate.

Time Event
Nov 9 Two domains later tied to the attack are registered
Nov 13 Hudson Rock sees similar code on three other web services
Nov 16, 05:23 The payload server's domain is registered
Nov 16, 08:10 The first crypto clipper build appears
Nov 16, 13:03 Stolen funds are swept to exchanges
Nov 16, ~17:56 The last payload variant goes live after several edits
Nov 16, 20:40–21:10 Mass cleanup of infected snippets, Ledger's at 20:41
Nov 16, 21:52 One infected snippet is still live

What the companies said

Optimizely said it blocked access to the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts and notified customers. It's still investigating.

Ledger said the issue on its site is fixed and that it doesn't affect Ledger devices or users' private keys (The Block). That's consistent with the analyses: the attack hit the website layer, not the signing device.

How much was stolen

On-chain, not much. Report URI put the amount that reached attacker wallets at about $7,000 by Monday evening. StepSecurity's update the next day estimated about $6,600 across eight attacker wallets, four of which never received anything. Card numbers, cookies and phone compromises don't show up on-chain, so the real damage is unknown and probably a lot higher.

Why this hits crypto products harder

A stolen card can be blocked and the charge disputed. A crypto transfer to a swapped address is final. There's no chargeback, and the user usually notices only when the funds don't arrive.

The attack also abuses the exact habit we teach. Don't type addresses by hand, copy them from a source you trust. On November 16 the trusted source was the official website of a hardware wallet company.

And nothing looks broken. The page renders, the address looks like an address, the transaction confirms. From the user's side, everything worked.

Why the usual defenses didn't stop it

Content Security Policy

CSP lets you list which origins may serve scripts. It's the first thing people mention after an injection, and it's worth having. But here the malicious code came from Optimizely's own domain, which every affected site had allowed on purpose. A policy like this would have let it through:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' https://cdn.optimizely.com

CSP still helps against other injections, and its reporting endpoint can tell you when unexpected scripts show up. It just can't protect you from a domain you've chosen to trust.

Subresource Integrity

SRI pins a script to a known hash, so the browser refuses to run it if the file changes:

<script
  src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.min.js"
  integrity="sha384-..."
  crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

That works for a library version that never changes. An experimentation snippet changes every time someone edits a test, which is the whole point of it, so in practice nobody pins it. It's a useful exercise to list which third-party scripts on your site can't be pinned. Those are the ones that can change without a deploy.

What to change if your product shows an address

1. Keep marketing scripts off sensitive pages

Deposit addresses, withdrawal forms and payment fields don't need A/B tests. The simplest fix is to not load experimentation, analytics or chat widgets there at all.

If you load them from your own code, a route check is enough to start:

const SENSITIVE_PATHS = ['/deposit', '/withdraw', '/checkout', '/send'];

const isSensitive = SENSITIVE_PATHS.some((path) =>
  window.location.pathname.startsWith(path)
);

if (!isSensitive) {
  loadExperimentScript(); // your Optimizely / analytics loader
}

Then back it up with a strict policy on those routes, so a script added through a tag manager later can't slip in:

Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.yourapp.com; frame-ancestors 'none'; report-to csp-reports

A stronger option is to move these flows to a separate subdomain, like pay.yourapp.com, that only ever loads your own code. The OWASP cheat sheet on third-party JavaScript goes deeper into isolation options like this one.

2. Know what runs on those pages

Keep a short inventory of third-party scripts per route, and monitor it. CSP reporting, a script monitoring service or a scheduled check that compares the scripts on /deposit against an allowlist all work. This campaign was spotted by people who watch scripts across many sites, not by the affected sites.

3. Give users a second way to check the address

Long hex strings are hard to compare. Split the address into groups so people can actually read it:

function groupAddress(address, size = 4) {
  return address.match(new RegExp(`.{1,${size}}`, 'g')).join(' ');
}

groupAddress('0x52908400098527886E0F7030069857D2E4169EE7');
// "0x52 9084 0009 8527 886E 0F70 3006 9857 D2E4 169E E7"

Show a QR code next to it, and where you can, confirm the address in a place the web page can't touch: the hardware wallet screen, the mobile app, or an email.

4. Treat pasted addresses as untrusted

If your app accepts an address from the clipboard (the paste event gives you the raw text), show it back clearly before sending, and warn when it doesn't match anything the user has saved:

addressInput.addEventListener('paste', (event) => {
  const pasted = event.clipboardData.getData('text').trim();
  const known = savedAddresses.includes(pasted);

  showConfirmation({
    address: groupAddress(pasted),
    warning: known ? null : 'This address is not in your saved list. Check every character.',
  });
});

To be honest about the limits: a malicious script running on the same page can patch these checks too. They're speed bumps for clipboard malware on the user's device. The real fix for this incident is point 1.

What users can do

For the person sending money, the habit that would have caught this is simple: check the whole address before you confirm, not just the first and last few characters. Clipboard malware and address poisoning both work best on people who only glance at the edges. This wallet security checklist covers it, along with a few other habits worth having, like keeping a separate low-balance wallet for unfamiliar dApps.

If you sent crypto on November 16 after copying an address from a big brand's website, compare the destination with the address you meant to use.

The takeaway

Your page is only as safe as the most permissive script on it. If that page shows a deposit address, your A/B testing tool has the same power over it as your own code. Decide which pages actually need it.

Sources

  • CoinDesk: Hackers planted crypto-stealing code on 178 organizations' sites, including HSBC, BBC and Ledger
  • Bitcoin.com: Hackers Hit Ledger and 177 Other Brands With a Crypto Address-Swapping Attack
  • Shattered.io: Optimjack Crypto Malware, 178 Sites, $6,600 Stolen
  • The Block: Ledger's statement on the Optimizely incident
  • Cointelegraph: malware swapping crypto addresses on 178 major websites

articles.title: Most of My Users Couldn't Sign In With Google, and It Wasn't My Bug
articles.description: Google refuses sign-in inside the X, Instagram and Facebook in-app browsers. My analytics showed it, my error logs hid it.
articles.body_html:
On 3 November I looked at 14 days of visitor data for one form on my site.

Five people had started filling it in and never finished. Four of them had pressed Continue with Google. Then nothing. They never came back.

The button itself wasn't broken. So where did they go?

Where they came from

My site is TrustCheck, and a lot of our visitors arrive from links shared on X, Instagram and Facebook.

When you tap a link inside those apps, it doesn't open Chrome or Safari. It opens the app's own built-in browser. And Google refuses to sign people in inside those built-in browsers. The person taps the button, gets an error page from Google, and closes the tab.

From my side, nothing failed. No error. No log line. Just a person who left.

The errors I was ignoring

What made it worse: I had been looking at errors from those same browsers for days, and filing them as junk.

My visitor insights kept recording "page errors" like:

Can't find variable: CONFIG
currentInset
webkit.messageHandlers

None of that is my code. The X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in-app browsers inject their own scripts into every page, and those scripts throw errors. On 1 November I filtered them out so they'd stop polluting my error counts:

public static function isNoise(?string $label): bool
{
    return (bool) preg_match(
        '/CONFIG|currentInset|webkit\.messageHandlers|__gCrWeb|instantSearchSDKJSBridge|WeixinJSBridge/',
        (string) $label
    );
}

Two days later I found out the same browsers were also quietly breaking my sign-in. The noise was a clue, and I had filtered it away.

The fix: a code by email

I didn't want to fight Google's rules. So I added a second way in that never leaves the site: type your email, get a 6-digit code, type it back.

Email code is now the first option on that form. Google is second.

The parts I cared about:

  • The code lives for 10 minutes, stored hashed, never in plain text.
  • 5 wrong tries and the code is dead.
  • At most 3 codes per email address in 10 minutes, so nobody can use the form to flood someone's inbox. 
$code = (string) random_int(100000, 999999);

Cache::put(self::key($email), [
    'hash'  => password_hash($code, PASSWORD_DEFAULT),
    'tries' => 0,
    'sent'  => $recent,
], 600);

Checking it uses password_verify() and deletes the code on success, so it can't be used twice.

On my laptop the code is written to the log instead of being emailed. I never want a test run to email a real person.

What I'd check on your site

If any of your traffic comes from social media, open your own site from inside the X or Instagram app and try to sign in. It takes two minutes.

I only saw this because I was counting where people stopped, not just what errored.

Have you found a bug that only happens inside in-app browsers? What was it?

articles.title: uBlock Origin's picker flaw and the authorization fix explained
articles.description: uBlock Origin patched a website-driven picker flaw. Learn the Firefox prerequisites, why the first fix failed, and why installed versions matter.
articles.body_html:
uBlock Origin patched a website-driven element-picker flaw that could let a hostile webpage save trusted filters. Those filters could run script in another site's context. For developers, the useful part of the story is the authority boundary: an interface owned by an extension can be reachable from a page while still needing to reject that page's commands. The maintainer's repair history shows why protecting an address was an incomplete answer.

TL;DR

  • The maintainer advisory lists 1.75.2 and lower as affected and 1.75.4 as patched. GitHub and Mozilla currently list stable 1.76.4. Use normal extension controls to update and check what is installed.
  • The documented path concerns Firefox MV2, a relevant resource-serving filtering rule, and a user click. Keep those conditions attached to the claim.
  • The first request-method hardening was bypassable. The next repair required a verified secret token to launch the picker.
  • The researcher explicitly says he did not build the hidden click overlay. His report and the advisory provide no victim count or evidence of active exploitation.

What the uBlock Origin element picker can authorize

The element picker lets a user choose an unwanted page element and create a blocking rule. Its convenience comes from keeping the interaction near the content the user wants to change. According to Smitty van Bodegom's report, its interface is an extension resource embedded over the webpage, and that interface can communicate with the extension background process to add filters.

That arrangement puts two different kinds of authority next to each other. The website supplies the content being inspected. The extension owns the tool that changes blocking behavior. A viewer can see one page-sized experience while the software needs to preserve a much stricter distinction between the parties inside it.

The report says rules added through the picker were treated as trusted, at least until recompilation. Some trusted filters can inject JavaScript into a matching page. Saving such a rule is therefore a consequential action. It can influence what happens when a different site is opened, beyond the element the user appeared to select.

I would review a feature like this by tracing the authority attached to the saved state. Who owns the interface? Which component accepts its messages? What happens to the rule after it reaches storage? Those questions expose the consequence that a tidy user interface can hide. In this episode's conceptual diagram, the page, picker and filter store stay separate so the transfer of authority remains visible.

How the reported path crossed a website boundary

A filtering feature could return an extension resource as a substitute for an unwanted network response. Van Bodegom describes this as supplying a harmless replacement for a script the website expects. The goal was compatibility while blocking unwanted content.

The same resource path could expose the extension's random internal identifier. Once a hostile page knew the internal address, it could load the picker interface and send it messages. The report describes an insufficiently checked input that could add another rule beyond the ordinary choice presented by the interface.

That second rule could reach the trusted filter store. It could target another website and execute script in that site's context. This is the boundary crossing behind the report's universal cross-site scripting terminology. The extension had authority to affect matching sites, and the hostile page could borrow that authority through the picker.

This explanation deliberately stays at the level of ownership, messages and saved state. We have not run the demonstration, installed an old extension, created a malicious filter or tested a real account. The video uses conceptual objects and a genuine recording of the public advisory's non-operational header. Neither is a claim that our show reproduced the exploit.

Firefox prerequisites and the click evidence

The advisory's summary identifies the Firefox MV2 extension, a relevant scriptlet filter that supplies an extension resource, and a user click. A vulnerability headline becomes less useful when those prerequisites disappear. Someone checking their own browser needs the correct product, architecture and installed version.

Van Bodegom also mentions a similar but less problematic issue in uBlock Origin Lite. That is a separate version and architecture. The statement supports acknowledging a related issue; it supplies no blanket conclusion that every MV3 extension is safe, or that every browser has the same reported path.

The user click is especially important to the evidence. The researcher describes making the embedded picker invisible or covering it so an ordinary click activates its Create button. He explicitly says he did not implement that hidden-overlay portion. The demonstrated ability to control the picker and the proposed way of disguising the click are distinct parts of his account.

The sources provide no victim count or evidence of active exploitation. That absence limits what we can say from this material. It cannot establish that no attack has ever occurred. I would preserve the qualification in summaries, captions and translated metadata rather than replacing it with a confident claim about all users.

Why recompilation was a weak cleanup boundary

The researcher says recompiling filters could clear the added rule's trusted status. That gives the story a tempting escape route: perhaps a later edit repairs the state before it matters. He also points out that the attacking page could immediately open the target page.

Those events have an order. The rule can be saved, the target page can be opened, and a later change can cause recompilation. A cleanup event occurring after the consequence has started offers a poor foundation for the authorization guarantee. Our diagram shows that ordering without assigning invented milliseconds or claiming a race measurement.

For an extension feature that saves privileged state, I would want the permission decision before the state change. A subsequent recompile can still have useful behavior, but its existence does not explain why an untrusted caller was permitted to create the rule in the first place. The repair history returns to exactly that question.

Why the first fix left the picker open

Hill's advisory records the private report on November 1 and a first hardening change published in 1.75.2 on November 2. Its title is "Avoid use of potentially tainted XHR methods in scriptlets." The email exchange then records a bypass that could still expose the internal identifier through another part of the request machinery.

Closing one route to a hidden address left a powerful interface reachable through another route. More importantly, the picker still needed a reliable way to distinguish its legitimate extension flow from a hostile page. The second repair addressed that launch boundary.

The November 3 change, released in 1.75.4, is titled "Launch element picker only with a verified secret token." The legitimate flow supplies authorization, and the picker checks it. A page knowing the resource address alone should remain outside the permission boundary.

Later changes in 1.76.0 validated proposed filters and restricted resource-related filters. They add protection around what gets saved and which resources filters can use. The selected advisory still names 1.75.4 as patched. The newer 1.76.4 release describes additional reported security work, and the official Mozilla listing currently offers that stable version. These statements have different scopes; preserve each one's meaning.

Model-assisted finding, human verification

Van Bodegom says he supplied a suspicion about filter injection to GPT-5.6 Sol, which found the issue. He checked and verified the result. He also says Claude wrote much of the demonstration code, while he wrote the report's prose himself.

Those are useful details about the author's workflow. They provide no independent benchmark of autonomous security research. I would keep the verified report, the maintainer's acknowledgment and the installable fixes as the receipts that matter to the user. A debate about model rankings can easily crowd out the concrete permission check the repair added.

Verdict: SHIP IT

I'd ship the patched picker because it checks authorization at the control boundary, and I'd keep the current stable extension installed. Future security work stays open. The early update advice belongs alongside the explanation, rather than being held until the end of a security story.

For other privileged extension interfaces, I would ask who is allowed to command the interface and change persistent state. Reachability is one property to inspect. The caller's authority is another property that needs its own explicit answer.

FAQ

Which uBlock Origin version should I check? The advisory's patched baseline is 1.75.4, while GitHub and Mozilla currently list stable 1.76.4. Check the version actually installed through the browser's normal extension controls and use the current stable release.

Was the issue a zero-click attack on every browser? The documented path required a click and a relevant resource-serving filter in Firefox MV2. The report discusses Lite separately. We performed no exploit test.

What changed after the first hardening? The November 3 repair required a verified secret token for picker launch. Later changes added proposed-filter validation and resource-related restrictions.

Did an AI discover and exploit this without a person? The author says a model found the issue after he supplied a hypothesis, and he verified it. That account supplies no independent autonomous-research benchmark. The hidden-overlay click trap was described but not built by him.

Sources

  • Smitty van Bodegom's report
  • Maintainer advisory and chronology
  • uBlock Origin 1.76.4 release
  • Official Mozilla listing
  • Hacker News discussion
