articles.title: TypeScript `protected` vs `private` in 2026: The Inheritance Visibility Rules That Bite Teams Mid-Refactor
articles.description: TypeScript's protected and private modifiers look similar but enforce wildly different visibility rules during inheritance. Teams hit these constraints mid-refactor when subclass access patterns suddenly break type checking.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript protected vs private in 2026: The Inheritance Visibility Rules That Bite Teams Mid-Refactor

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The Access Modifier Confusion That Breaks Refactors

Teams discover the difference between protected and private when a seemingly safe refactor suddenly fails type checking. A developer extracts shared logic into a base class, marks a field private, and watches the entire subclass hierarchy reject access to that field. The build breaks. The refactor stalls. The team backtracks to public and ships the leaky abstraction.

The problem: private members vanish the moment inheritance enters the picture. Subclasses cannot touch them. The TypeScript compiler enforces this boundary strictly, treating private as a hard contract between the declaring class and no one else. When developers expect inheritance-friendly visibility, they reach for the wrong modifier and hit a wall mid-refactor.

Problem diagram showing private field blocking subclass access

The solution: protected members expose themselves to the inheritance chain. Subclasses gain access. The refactor proceeds without visibility violations. The type checker passes because the modifier matches the actual access pattern.

Solution diagram showing protected field allowing subclass access

This matters because the wrong choice compounds during maintenance. A private field that should have been protected forces awkward workarounds (public getters, reflection tricks, or abandoning inheritance entirely). Teams that understand the visibility rules ship cleaner hierarchies and avoid the mid-refactor panic when TypeScript refuses to compile.

Key Takeaways

  • private members are invisible to subclasses; only the declaring class can access them, making them unsuitable for inheritance-based patterns.
  • protected members expose themselves to the entire inheritance chain, allowing subclasses to access and override them while still hiding them from external code.
  • TypeScript's structural typing treats private as a nominal constraint: two classes with identically named private fields are incompatible even if their shapes match.
  • Both private and protected disappear during compilation to JavaScript; the runtime offers zero enforcement, making these purely compile-time contracts.
  • Choosing the wrong modifier mid-refactor forces visibility violations that break builds and require either exposing fields as public or redesigning the hierarchy.

How protected and private Actually Work: The Visibility Rules

TypeScript's access modifiers control compile-time visibility, not runtime behavior. The TypeScript handbook defines three visibility levels: public (accessible everywhere, the default), protected (accessible within the class and its subclasses), and private (accessible only within the declaring class). These boundaries exist solely during type checking.

A private member creates a one-class perimeter. The declaring class can read and write it. Subclasses cannot. External code cannot. The TypeScript compiler enforces this by rejecting any access outside the declaring class:

class DatabaseConnection {
  private credentials: string;

  constructor(creds: string) {
    this.credentials = creds; // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }

  connect() {
    console.log(`Connecting with ${this.credentials}`);
  }
}

class SecureConnection extends DatabaseConnection {
  audit() {
    console.log(this.credentials); // ✗ Property 'credentials' is private
  }
}

The subclass SecureConnection inherits the structure of DatabaseConnection, but the private modifier blocks access. The compiler sees the reference to this.credentials and rejects it. The error message is explicit: Property 'credentials' is private and only accessible within class 'DatabaseConnection'.

A protected member expands the perimeter to include the inheritance chain. The declaring class and all subclasses can access it. External code still cannot. This matches the common pattern where base classes define fields that subclasses need to implement specialized behavior:

class Cache {
  protected storage: Map<string, unknown>;

  constructor() {
    this.storage = new Map(); // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key); // ✓ allowed in declaring class
  }
}

class LRUCache extends Cache {
  private accessOrder: string[] = [];

  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.storage.get(key); // ✓ allowed in subclass
    this.accessOrder.push(key);
    return value;
  }
}

The protected field storage is visible to both Cache and LRUCache. The subclass can directly read the map to implement custom eviction logic. The external API remains unchanged because protected still hides the field from consumers of the class.

TypeScript visibility diagram showing access modifier boundaries

TypeScript does not allow cross-hierarchy protected access. A subclass can access protected members on this, but not on sibling class instances. This prevents a Derived1 instance from reaching into a Derived2 instance's protected state, even though both extend the same base class. The TypeScript handbook explains this as a safeguard against unintended coupling between unrelated subclasses.

The visibility rules create a hierarchy of access: private locks the field to one class, protected extends visibility to descendants, and public removes restrictions entirely. Developers choose based on how the field participates in inheritance.

The Structural Typing Trap: Why private Members Break Type Compatibility

TypeScript uses structural typing for most type checks. Two objects with identical shapes are compatible, regardless of where they were declared. The compiler compares properties, not names or origins. A { x: number } from one file matches a { x: number } from another.

private and protected members break this rule. The TypeScript compiler treats them nominally: two types are compatible only if their private or protected members come from the same declaration. The TypeScript handbook states this explicitly: "For two types to be considered compatible, if one of them has a private member, then the other must have a private member that originated in the same declaration."

This creates surprising incompatibility between structurally identical classes:

class Animal {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

class Employee {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

const animal: Animal = new Animal("Dog");
const employee: Employee = new Employee("Alice");

const entity: Animal = employee; // ✗ Type 'Employee' is not assignable to type 'Animal'

Both Animal and Employee have a private name: string field. The shapes are identical. Structural typing would treat them as compatible. The compiler rejects the assignment because the private members originated in different declarations. The name in Animal and the name in Employee are distinct, incompatible types.

Inheritance preserves the declaration origin. A subclass that extends a base class inherits the base's private and protected members, including their declaration origin. This makes the subclass compatible with the base:

class Animal {
  private name: string;
  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name: string) {
    super(name);
  }
}

const animal: Animal = new Dog("Rex"); // ✓ compatible via inheritance

The private name in Dog originated in Animal. The compiler sees the shared origin and allows the assignment. This nominal check ensures that private members remain truly private: only classes in the same inheritance chain can share them.

This matters during refactors. Extracting a base class with private fields breaks compatibility with any external code that expects the original type. The structural shape remains identical, but the declaration origin changes. Type checks that previously passed now fail.

The workaround: use protected for fields that participate in inheritance, or avoid access modifiers entirely for fields that need structural compatibility.

protected vs private in Inheritance Hierarchies: Real Refactoring Scenarios

Teams hit the protected versus private decision when pulling shared state into a base class. The question: should subclasses access this field directly, or only through methods?

A common scenario: multiple service classes share database connection logic. The initial implementation duplicates the connection field in each class. The refactor extracts a BaseService with the shared connection. The developer marks it private to enforce encapsulation:

class BaseService {
  private connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }

  protected query(sql: string): Promise<unknown[]> {
    return this.connection.execute(sql);
  }
}

class UserService extends BaseService {
  async findById(id: number): Promise<User | null> {
    // Must use this.query() instead of direct connection access
    const rows = await this.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}`);
    return rows[0] as User;
  }
}

The private connection forces subclasses to use the protected query() method. This works when the base class API covers all use cases. It breaks when a subclass needs direct connection access for transaction management, connection pooling, or custom query building. The refactor stalls. The developer either exposes connection as public (leaking the abstraction) or redesigns the base class API to support every possible use case (overengineering).

The alternative: mark connection as protected. Subclasses gain direct access. The base class still hides it from external code:

class BaseService {
  protected connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }
}

class TransactionalUserService extends BaseService {
  async createWithAudit(user: User): Promise<void> {
    const tx = await this.connection.beginTransaction(); // ✓ direct access
    try {
      await tx.execute("INSERT INTO users ...");
      await tx.execute("INSERT INTO audit_log ...");
      await tx.commit();
    } catch (error) {
      await tx.rollback();
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

The subclass uses the connection directly for transaction control. The base class does not need to anticipate every transaction pattern. The protected modifier trusts subclasses to use the connection correctly.

Inheritance hierarchy showing protected field access patterns

Another scenario: a Component base class manages lifecycle state. Subclasses need to read the current state to decide whether to run certain logic. The developer marks state private and adds a getter:

class Component {
  private state: "mounted" | "unmounted" = "unmounted";

  mount() {
    this.state = "mounted";
    this.onMount();
  }

  protected onMount() {
    // hook for subclasses
  }

  isMounted(): boolean {
    return this.state === "mounted";
  }
}

class AsyncComponent extends Component {
  protected onMount() {
    if (this.isMounted()) { // must call getter
      this.loadData();
    }
  }
}

The getter works, but adds indirection. Every subclass that checks state calls isMounted() instead of reading state directly. If the state shape becomes more complex (adding "mounting", "unmounting", "error" states), the base class must add corresponding getters for each state. This scales poorly.

The protected alternative eliminates the getter:

class Component {
  protected state: "mounted" | "unmounted" = "unmounted";

  mount() {
    this.state = "mounted";
    this.onMount();
  }

  protected onMount() {}
}

class AsyncComponent extends Component {
  protected onMount() {
    if (this.state === "mounted") { // direct access
      this.loadData();
    }
  }
}

Subclasses read state directly. The base class does not proliferate getters. The tradeoff: subclasses can mutate state incorrectly. The developer trusts that subclass authors understand the lifecycle contract.

Runtime Reality: Why Both Modifiers Disappear in Compiled JavaScript

TypeScript's access modifiers exist only during type checking. The compiler strips them during transpilation. The emitted JavaScript contains no enforcement, no runtime checks, and no access restrictions. A private field becomes an ordinary property accessible via bracket notation or reflection.

The TypeScript handbook states this explicitly: "Like other aspects of TypeScript's type system, private and protected are only enforced during type checking." The compiled output looks identical for public, protected, and private fields.

class Secure {
  private secret: string;
  protected internal: string;
  public visible: string;

  constructor() {
    this.secret = "hidden";
    this.internal = "shared";
    this.visible = "open";
  }
}

The TypeScript compiler targeting ES2015 emits:

class Secure {
  constructor() {
    this.secret = "hidden";
    this.internal = "shared";
    this.visible = "open";
  }
}

All three fields appear as regular properties. No visibility enforcement. A consumer can access secret and internal directly:

const instance = new Secure();
console.log(instance.secret); // "hidden" — no runtime error
console.log(instance["secret"]); // "hidden" — bracket notation bypasses TypeScript

The TypeScript compiler rejects these accesses during type checking, but the runtime allows them. This creates a disconnect: code that fails to compile still runs successfully if the type checks are bypassed.

JavaScript's #private syntax (standardized in ES2022) provides runtime enforcement. Fields declared with # are truly private: the JavaScript engine prevents external access:

class Secure {
  #secret = "hidden";

  getSecret() {
    return this.#secret; // ✓ internal access allowed
  }
}

const instance = new Secure();
console.log(instance.#secret); // SyntaxError: Private field '#secret' must be declared

The # syntax creates hard privacy. The engine throws an error at runtime, not just during compilation. TypeScript supports this syntax and treats #private fields as truly inaccessible.

Feature TypeScript private TypeScript protected JavaScript #private
Compile-time enforcement Yes (TypeScript only) Yes (TypeScript only) Yes (TypeScript only)
Runtime enforcement No No Yes (JavaScript engine)
Subclass access Blocked Allowed Blocked
External access via bracket notation Allowed at runtime Allowed at runtime Blocked
Transpilation to ES5 Becomes public property Becomes public property Polyfilled with WeakMap

Comparison diagram showing TypeScript private versus JavaScript private fields

Teams that need runtime privacy use #private fields. Teams that need inheritance-friendly visibility use protected. Teams that want compile-time guardrails without runtime overhead stick with TypeScript's private and accept the soft enforcement.

The practical implication: access modifiers are documentation for the type checker and other developers. They communicate intent (this field should not leak outside the class), but they do not prevent malicious or careless access at runtime. Security-critical code requires additional runtime validation.

When to Reach for protected vs private: Decision Framework for 2026

The choice between protected and private depends on whether subclasses need field access. The decision tree starts with one question: will any subclass need to read or write this field directly?

If no subclass needs access, use private. This signals that the field is an implementation detail of the declaring class. Subclasses should not depend on it. Future refactors can change the field's type, name, or behavior without breaking subclasses:

class HttpClient {
  private retryCount: number = 0;
  private maxRetries: number = 3;

  async request(url: string): Promise<Response> {
    while (this.retryCount < this.maxRetries) {
      try {
        return await fetch(url);
      } catch (error) {
        this.retryCount++;
      }
    }
    throw new Error("Max retries exceeded");
  }
}

The retryCount and maxRetries fields manage retry logic internal to HttpClient. No subclass needs to know about them. Marking them private allows the developer to replace the retry mechanism (switching to exponential backoff, for example) without touching subclass code.

If subclasses need access, use protected. This signals that the field participates in the inheritance contract. Subclasses can read and write it to implement specialized behavior:

class Repository {
  protected cache: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  get(key: string): unknown | undefined {
    return this.cache.get(key);
  }

  set(key: string, value: unknown): void {
    this.cache.set(key, value);
  }
}

class TTLRepository extends Repository {
  private expirations: Map<string, number> = new Map();

  set(key: string, value: unknown, ttl: number): void {
    this.cache.set(key, value); // ✓ direct cache access
    this.expirations.set(key, Date.now() + ttl);
  }

  get(key: string): unknown | undefined {
    const expiration = this.expirations.get(key);
    if (expiration && Date.now() > expiration) {
      this.cache.delete(key); // ✓ direct cache access
      this.expirations.delete(key);
      return undefined;
    }
    return this.cache.get(key);
  }
}

The protected cache allows TTLRepository to implement expiration logic without duplicating the storage mechanism. The base class trusts subclasses to maintain cache consistency.

Scenario Use private Use protected
Field is pure implementation detail ✓
Subclasses will never need access ✓
Field participates in overridable behavior ✓
Subclasses need direct read/write access ✓
Future subclasses are unknown but likely ✓
Field type may change in future versions ✓

Decision flowchart for choosing between protected and private

A common pattern: use private for fields that drive internal algorithms, and protected for fields that represent shared state. If the field's value affects how subclasses implement their behavior, make it protected. If the field exists only to support the base class's methods, make it private.

The exception: library code intended for public consumption. Public APIs often expose hooks (like React component lifecycle methods) but keep all state private. This prevents consumers from accidentally breaking the library's invariants. The library provides protected methods for subclass customization, but keeps data fields locked.

Migration Patterns: Fixing Mid-Refactor Visibility Violations Without Breaking Everything

Teams discover visibility violations mid-refactor when a subclass suddenly cannot access a field that was previously visible. The fix depends on whether the field should have been protected from the start, or whether the subclass access pattern was a mistake.

The first migration: promoting private to protected. This happens when a developer correctly identified shared state but chose the wrong modifier. The fix is mechanical: change private to protected in the base class. TypeScript recompiles without errors. Subclasses gain access:

// Before: private blocks subclass access
class EventEmitter {
  private listeners: Map<string, Function[]> = new Map();

  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || [];
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
  }
}

class LoggingEmitter extends EventEmitter {
  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    console.log(`Registering ${event}`);
    // Need to access this.listeners but it's private
  }
}

// After: protected allows subclass access
class EventEmitter {
  protected listeners: Map<string, Function[]> = new Map();

  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || [];
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
  }
}

class LoggingEmitter extends EventEmitter {
  on(event: string, handler: Function) {
    console.log(`Registering ${event}`);
    const handlers = this.listeners.get(event) || []; // ✓ now allowed
    handlers.push(handler);
    this.listeners.set(event, handlers);
    super.on(event, handler);
  }
}

The migration preserves the external API. Code that uses EventEmitter continues working. Only subclass implementations change.

The second migration: demoting protected to private with an accessor layer. This happens when subclass access was a mistake. The base class wants to change the field's implementation without breaking subclasses. The fix: add a protected getter/setter and mark the field private:

// Before: protected exposes implementation detail
class Cache {
  protected storage: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key);
  }
}

class MetricsCache extends Cache {
  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.storage.get(key); // direct access
    this.recordHit();
    return value;
  }
}

// After: private field with protected accessor
class Cache {
  private storage: Map<string, unknown> = new Map();

  protected getFromStorage(key: string): unknown {
    return this.storage.get(key);
  }

  get(key: string): unknown {
    return this.getFromStorage(key);
  }
}

class MetricsCache extends Cache {
  get(key: string): unknown {
    const value = this.getFromStorage(key); // accessor method
    this.recordHit();
    return value;
  }
}

The base class can now replace storage (switching from Map to WeakMap, for example) without breaking subclasses. The protected accessor method abstracts the storage mechanism.

Migration flowchart for fixing visibility violations

The third migration: extracting a new base class when visibility boundaries conflict. This happens when multiple subclasses need different access to the same field. The fix: create an intermediate base class with looser visibility, and derive restrictive subclasses from it:

// Problem: some subclasses need access, others don't
class Service {
  private connection: DatabaseConnection; // too restrictive
}

class AuditService extends Service {
  // Needs connection access but can't get it
}

class ReadOnlyService extends Service {
  // Doesn't need connection access
}

// Solution: intermediate base class with protected access
abstract class ConnectedService {
  protected connection: DatabaseConnection;

  constructor(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
    this.connection = conn;
  }
}

class AuditService extends ConnectedService {
  async log(event: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.connection.execute("INSERT INTO audit ..."); // ✓ allowed
  }
}

class ReadOnlyService extends ConnectedService {
  // Can access connection but chooses not to
}

The intermediate class ConnectedService exposes the connection to its subclasses. Subclasses that need direct access derive from it. Subclasses that do not derive from a wrapper that hides it.

The key: migrate incrementally. Change one modifier at a time. Run the type checker after each change. Avoid bulk find-and-replace operations that change visibility across dozens of classes simultaneously. Each modifier change is a contract change. Subclasses may depend on the existing contract in subtle ways.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a subclass override a private field from the base class?

No, subclasses cannot access private fields at all. TypeScript treats private as a strict boundary: only the declaring class can read or write the field. A subclass that declares a field with the same name creates a separate, unrelated field. The base class field remains hidden and inaccessible.

Does protected allow access from outside the inheritance chain?

No, protected members are visible only within the class and its subclasses. External code (code that does not extend the class) cannot access protected members. The visibility is strictly limited to the inheritance hierarchy, not to arbitrary code that imports the class.

Why does TypeScript reject assignment between structurally identical classes with private fields?

TypeScript uses nominal typing for private and protected members. Two classes with private fields of the same type and name are incompatible unless they share the same inheritance chain. This prevents accidental mixing of unrelated types that happen to have structurally similar private state.

Can I use protected in an interface?

No, TypeScript interfaces cannot declare protected members. Interfaces define public contracts for objects. Access modifiers like protected and private apply only to class declarations. If you need a contract that includes protected members, use an abstract class instead of an interface.

What happens to protected fields when compiling to JavaScript?

TypeScript strips all access modifiers during transpilation. A protected field becomes a regular public property in the emitted JavaScript. The runtime offers no enforcement. Any code can access the field using direct property access or bracket notation, regardless of the original TypeScript visibility.

Conclusion: Choosing the Right Access Modifier Before Your Team Hits the Wall

The difference between protected and private determines whether subclasses can access base class state. Choosing private locks the field to the declaring class. Choosing protected exposes it to the inheritance chain. Teams that understand this distinction before refactoring avoid mid-build visibility violations and the forced choice between leaky abstractions and redesigned hierarchies. The decision starts with one question: will subclasses need this field? The answer dictates the modifier.

Sources

  • TypeScript: Documentation - JSDoc Reference

articles.title: I built an AI whiteboard that draws on the board instead of answering in chat
articles.description: One sentence in, an AWS architecture out: real cloud icons, attached connectors and a plain JSON file. With the full trace of one run.
articles.body_html:
Ask a chatbot for an architecture diagram and you get a block of Mermaid. You paste it somewhere else, the layout is off, the icons are grey boxes, and the thing that made the drawing is not the thing you fix it in.

I wanted the model to work on the same canvas I do, with the same tools I have, so that what it makes is ordinary shapes I can drag around afterwards. That became Whiboard: an online whiteboard for diagrams and plans, with an assistant that draws on the board.

There is a try page that opens a real board with no account. This post is one run on that page from start to finish: the prompt, every step the assistant took (including the one that failed), and the files that came out.

One sentence in

Draw the architecture of a web app on AWS: CloudFront in front, a load balancer, two app servers, Postgres on RDS, Redis for sessions and S3 for uploads.

It took 1 minute 22 seconds, and I did not touch the result. Here is the same board in the app:

I asked for the six services. It added the users, a VPC, an Auto Scaling group around the two servers and labels like "HTTPS" and "uploads" on its own. You may or may not want those, and it hardly matters, because none of this is a picture:

  • Every icon is a tile from the built-in library: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Cloudflare, plus brand, dev and Linux logos. Double-click a tile to swap it.
  • Every arrow is a connector attached to the shapes at both ends. Drag App Server 2 somewhere else and its arrows follow.
  • Everything the assistant does is an undo step. ⌘Z walks its work back piece by piece.

What it did in those 82 seconds

The panel lists each step while it works. This is the whole run, copied from it:

✓ Reading the board
✓ Searching icons for "cloudfront"
✓ Searching icons for "elastic load balancing"
✓ Searching icons for "ec2"
✓ Searching icons for "rds"
✓ Searching icons for "elasticache"
✓ Searching icons for "s3"
✓ Searching icons for "user"
✓ Searching icons for "simple storage service"
  Reasoning
✓ Drawing 8 nodes, 10 connections
✓ Looking at the board
  Reasoning
✓ Searching the board for "connector"
✓ Reading the board
  Reasoning
✓ Deleting 3 elements
✗ Drawing 0 nodes, 1 connections
  Nothing to draw: give at least one node, container or label.
✓ Reading the board
✓ Searching icons for "aws cloud"
✓ Adding 1 elements
✓ Changing 1 elements
✓ Looking at the board
  Reasoning
✓ Changing 2 elements
✓ Looking at the board

Answered in 1m 22s · first output after 1.7s · 11 steps

Three things in there are worth pointing at.

It finds real icons first. Before drawing anything it searches the icon library eight times, which is why the diagram has the actual CloudFront and RDS tiles and not rectangles with names in them.

It looks at its own work. "Looking at the board" renders the board to an image and hands it back to the model. After the first draft it looked, deleted three elements and went back in to fix them.

One step failed. The line marked ✗ is the drawing tool refusing a call that had a connection and no nodes. The model read the board again and got there another way. I left it in because that is what a real run looks like.

What else you can ask it

  • Change what is already there: "make every sticky about pricing orange and put them in one column", "turn these notes into a flowchart".
  • Read a file sitting on the board. Drop a spreadsheet, a CSV, a document or a deck on the canvas and ask "how many rows are in that CSV?" or "sum up the proposal".
  • Take an image or a video as input. A video is cut into at most ten still frames in your browser; the video itself is never uploaded.

Next to the assistant are three one-click tools: Summary (key points, decisions, action items, open questions), Organize (sorts a wall of sticky notes into themes) and Ideas.

The file is yours

The other thing I wanted from a whiteboard was to be able to leave it.

There are five export formats, and all five are on every plan, the free one included: PNG, SVG, PDF, draw.io and JSON. draw.io works both ways: drop a .drawio file on a board and it becomes editable shapes and connectors, then export it back when you are done. There is also an importer for Miro boards, through Miro's API.

The JSON is the whole board, never encrypted, in a documented shape. This is from the file the board above exported, cut down to two of its 58 elements:

{
  "app": "whiboard",
  "version": 1,
  "name": "My first board",
  "exportedAt": "2026-11-16T21:40:17.313Z",
  "elements": [
    {
      "id": "uUKJoRJgdRs8AkPi",
      "boardId": "try",
      "parentId": "ZKz_bMtgIxHS4zAc",
      "x": 162,
      "y": 137,
      "w": 76,
      "h": 76,
      "rotation": 0,
      "z": "aX",
      "style": {},
      "locked": false,
      "v": { "clock": 50, "actor": "try" },
      "type": "logo",
      "props": { "icon": "aws:AmazonCloudFront", "label": "CloudFront", "hideLabel": true }
    },
    {
      "id": "1JGJUcFwig1wBTPg",
      "boardId": "try",
      "parentId": null,
      "x": 0,
      "y": 0,
      "w": 0,
      "h": 0,
      "rotation": 0,
      "z": "a7",
      "style": {
        "stroke": "#4b5563",
        "strokeWidth": 1.5,
        "fontSize": 12,
        "fontFamily": "ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace",
        "color": "#4b5563"
      },
      "locked": false,
      "v": { "clock": 24, "actor": "try" },
      "type": "connector",
      "props": {
        "start": { "elId": "VKRUptdCE37irVRL", "anchor": "r" },
        "end": { "elId": "uUKJoRJgdRs8AkPi", "anchor": "l" },
        "route": "straight",
        "startArrow": "none",
        "endArrow": "arrow",
        "label": "HTTPS",
        "labelPos": "above"
      }
    }
  ]
}

It is a flat list. A connector names the ids of the two items it joins, here the Users tile and CloudFront. You can diff the file in Git, and the import accepts the same shape, so a script can write a board and you drop the file on the canvas.

Some things do not travel yet, and I would rather say so here than have you find out:

  • Uploaded images and videos are not inside the board JSON. Items point at them by id.
  • A .drawio export has no place for freehand strokes or images, and logo tiles arrive as labelled boxes without the icon. Use JSON or SVG to keep those.

The full list is on the no lock-in page.

If you would rather script it

An API. Everything the web app does goes through one HTTP API, with an OpenAPI 3.1 document at /api/v1/openapi.json and an interactive reference.

curl -s https://whiboard.com/api/v1/boards/$BOARD_ID/snapshot \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN"

Two caveats: there are no personal access tokens yet, so you sign in as a user like the app does, and the API is not versioned for third parties yet. The API guide has the details.

An iframe. An embed puts a whole board, one frame or an area of a board on another site, view only, and visitors need no account. Reloading the page shows the board as it is now, so the architecture diagram in your docs stops going stale.

<iframe src="https://embed.whiboard.com/embed/…" title="Architecture" width="100%" height="480"
  style="border:0;border-radius:12px" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe>

SVG in, shape out. Paste SVG markup on a board and its outline becomes a shape you can fill, resize, label and connect like any other.

How it is built, briefly

  • Browser: React 19 around a Canvas 2D engine written for this, with a spatial index and level-of-detail rendering. It holds 60 fps at 5,000 items, measured on a laptop.
  • Server: a Go API, a WebSocket hub with one room per board, Redis for pub/sub and presence, MongoDB for boards, ops and versions, and an S3 bucket for files.
  • Sync: every edit is an op. If two people change the same item, the later change wins. Lose the connection and you keep editing; the changes are sent when you are back.
  • Assistant: a Claude model with tools that act on the board: read it, search the icons, draw, change, delete, look at a render. The tools run in your browser against the live canvas, which is why each call is one undo step. The trace above is those tool calls.

What it costs

Free: unlimited boards, 5 editors, 3 AI prompts a day, no card. Team is $5 per editor a month. Viewers never pay.

What it is not

  • It is only a whiteboard. There are no docs, tasks or chat in it.
  • There is no mobile app.
  • There is no voting and no timer.
  • Two people cannot type in the same note at once. The later change wins.

Try it

whiboard.com/try opens a real board in your browser with nothing to sign up for. The assistant gives you 2 prompts per IP address there, so make them count. A free account gets 3 a day, and if you sign up from that page, the board you drew moves into your account.

I would like to know what it gets wrong. Give it the architecture you actually run and tell me in the comments where the diagram falls apart.

articles.title: The Manager Who Doesn't Use AI Has Already Lost: Soft Skills
articles.description: AI writes your minutes, rehearses your difficult conversations, and spots burnout before you do. How...
articles.body_html:
AI writes your minutes, rehearses your difficult conversations, and spots burnout before you do. How about you?

TL;DR: AI removes a manager's cognitive limit. Use it for meetings, feedback, and hard conversations.

This is the second part of the extended article version of my ninth talk at Nerdearla, in September 2026.

The first part covers the hard skills: managing the work.

The talk is in Spanish with English subtitles available.

Nerdbuster and Nerdflix

A quick recap, in case you skipped the first part.

Your job was to maintain Nerdbuster, a video rental system, in production in the 1990s.

Today, you maintain Nerdflix, a streaming platform for nerds, in production.

But one thing never changed:

A manager can't be everywhere at the same time.

Here's the thesis:

What happens when that cognitive limitation disappears?

How to Read This Article

Each section compares Nerdbuster and Nerdflix and uses these markers:

  • 🧩 A skill you can build for your AI assistant
  • 🧭 Human in the loop: the decision that stays with a person
  • ⚠️ A warning: consent, bias, law, or governance

Part 2: Managing People

Everything in the first part was technical.

Now comes the part they didn't teach me at computer science university.

This is outside my comfort zone.

I studied exact sciences, where the most emotional moment is a rounding error. I'm not the person with the best soft skills in the industry.

I had to build them as I became a manager.

AI matters even more nowadays for soft skills.

You move from managing the work to managing people.

Meetings

In Nerdbuster, meetings were crowded and informal.

No action items.

Chronic meeting-itis.

  • "I need you to talk to my customer."
  • "But I'm on another project."
  • "Come anyway."

There are plenty of memes about getting nothing done because you spend the whole day in meetings.

Someone wrote the minutes by hand. Nobody read them.

The minutes said: "Let's do this, and we'll see how."

In Nerdflix, only the relevant people must show up.

You check each attendee's career profile to confirm they can make the decision.

/meeting-profiles: decides who needs to attend. 🧩

The AI and the company brain support them.

You record and transcribe the meeting.

The transcript isn't literal.

With a template, you keep only what matters.

If you spend five minutes talking about football, the minutes skip it.

The AI writes down the minutes and the action items: who said what, what to do, and how you track it.

An architecture decision becomes an architecture decision record (ADR) directly.

/meeting-minutes: writes the transcript, the minutes, and the action items. 🧩

Scheduling happens automatically.

/find-timeslot: books the meeting automatically. 🧩

⚠️ Consent: You tell people when you record them.

🧭 Human in the loop: A person reviews the minutes before publishing them. Otherwise, someone could say "the AI wrote that action item". No. You did.

Managing Up and Stakeholders

In Nerdbuster, managing up meant guessing.

You guessed what your boss wanted to hear, and you showed up with the answer before they asked the question.

The result was a long, detailed report and a weekend lost to bureaucracy.

In Nerdflix, the AI translates the technical status into business impact.

One page. No jargon.

/executive-summary: fits the status on one page. 🧩

The AI is your sparring partner.

You use it in adversarial mode: "I have to say this, and a business person will sit in front of me."

The AI tells you if your tone and language fit that audience.

You can ask it to play an aggressive customer who pressures you commercially.

You train with AI sparring, and you walk in with your answers ready.

(I wish I had this when I started managing).

Managing up is no longer guessing.

It's communicating well and fast, in the language of the person who decides.

/translate-to-business-language: turns technical status into business impact. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: Reviewing your commitments is critical. The AI can't promise on your behalf.

Communications, Auto-Replies, and Alerts

In Nerdbuster, you wrote to a customer on long email.

You copied half the company, just in case.

The longer it was, the more serious it looked.

Email chains grew out of control. "RE: RE: RE:" until you lost count.

Photo by Antoni Shkraba from Pexels

Nobody tracked them, and nobody knew who should answer.

At some point, the thread faded away. Until someone brought it back.

There were no clear action items, but plenty of people in copy, each one hoarding the thread.

In Nerdflix, you write much shorter messages. Straight to the point.

/summarize-status: summarizes where each thread stands. 🧩

And there's something new: you don't know if a person or an AI agent reads your message on the other side.

You write differently, knowing that.

/adversarial-customer-role: plays a tough customer so you test your message before you send it. 🧩

The AI is your friend and also your foe.

😈 Inbox zero.

Your inbox isn't a to-do list.

You process everything that comes in:
-with a rule
-with the company brain
-with your attention-
-with an AI agent.

You work with empty backlogs.

The AI summarizes and prioritizes the threads and the alerts, and drafts the replies.

For routine messages, you can use an agent like OpenClaw or Hermes.

/triage-inbox: sorts and prioritizes your inbox. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: Every message carries your signature and your tone, not the plastic AI tone.

⚠️ Governance: Turning on auto-replies and reading confidential information is never your decision alone. It needs explicit approval from your organization governance and the least privilege possible. That makes it a governance decision. These agents aren't approved products in most companies. You should never upload confidential data to an AI your company hasn't approved. It can leak.

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager decides what gets automated and what doesn't.

Delegating

In Nerdbuster, delegating meant handing out tickets at the planning meeting.

You assigned them to whoever was available.

Or to whoever had fewer sticky notes on the whiteboard.

People were treated as interchangeable, fungible resources.

"I had a programmer. Another programmer arrived. Same thing."

You know people aren't the same and you should treat them kindly and individually. You should ban the word resource from your Taylorist language.

In Nerdflix, delegating well is something else.

You shouldn't say "you have to do this task".

You say: "This is for a critical customer. It goes to production in a week. We're late. Something else comes after it."

You explain the why to the AI. You explain it to people too.

You drop the Taylorist "do this as requested, never mind why".

Context empowers people. With enough autonomy, they take responsibility.

The context comes from the company brain.

/delegate-with-context: pulls the context from the company brain and structures the delegation. 🧩

The team takes ownership, with autonomy.

Open your AI model and type:

I need to organize the next Nerdflix sprint.

That's a mediocre prompt.

It's vague. It has no context and no constraints. It hands the whole decision over to the AI.

Now try something different:

ROLE: Act as the Engineering Manager of an 8-person team on Nerdflix.

CONTEXT:
We have 12 pending tickets.
Three of them impact customers.
Two of them block other work.
We have an external dependency that will probably arrive late.
The team is showing signs of burnout.
The project deadline can't move.

TASK: Help me decide what should go into the next sprint.

CONSTRAINT: Don't make the decision for me.
First, identify the relevant variables.
Then propose three different strategies.

OUTPUT: For each strategy, explain:
- What we gain
- What we sacrifice
- What risk we introduce
- What additional information we would need

Finally, challenge my decision.
Act as a manager who disagrees with me.

You didn't ask it to write a sprint.

You asked it to help you think.

That difference is huge.

If you don't want to build a skill, you should at least write structured prompts.

You don't carry that context in your head.

It comes from the company brain: the accumulated memory of decisions, post-mortems, and incidents.

It doesn't appear by magic. You build it, session after session.

The better you build it, the better you delegate, because you give both the AI and the human the why and not just the what.

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager decides what goes into the sprint.

Post-Mortems

In Nerdbuster, the post-mortem was a tense meeting.

Everybody looked for a scapegoat. 🐐 The winner was usually whoever missed the meeting.


Photo by Yan Krukau from Pexels

The informal notes got lost. Nobody left with clear action items.

That was a culture of fear.

In Nerdflix, the post-mortem is blameless.

You learn from the process and improve it.

The AI transcribes the ceremony and extracts concrete action items.

You cut any blaming live.

The action items belong to the team, not to people.

If a person needs to adjust something, you handle it in private, with journaling.

Good and bad cases feed the company brain.

/post-mortem-minutes: transcribes the ceremony and extracts the action items. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The facilitator cuts the blaming and rephrases it in generic terms, so nothing points at a person. A person reviews each case before it goes into the company brain.

Ceremonies: Stand-Ups, Retros, and Other Rituals

In Nerdbuster, the stand-up was literally standing up for thirty minutes.

It ended up as a status and time report.

Someone spent ten minutes explaining they had met with another team the day before. Everybody else was bored.

The retrospective was a wall of generic sticky notes: "what went well, what went wrong", with no real actions.

Photo by Mikhail Nilov from Pexels

In Nerdflix, the stand-up meeting is async.

Everybody writes. The AI builds the summary and flags real blockers.

You don't care what each person is doing.

You care about what's blocking them.

/standup-summary: summarizes the async stand-up and flags blockers. 🧩

Unblocking people is your job. Honestly, it's your only job.

A bit of informal chat is fine. You're human.

But if an update brings no action item and no blocker, nobody needs to hear it.

The AI also finds patterns across retrospectives.

It tells you, anonymously: "The last six meeting minutes mention that another team doesn't collaborate."

You don't need to ask. It detects the pattern. That's the agentic side of AI.

If a complaint repeats three times, it's a pattern, and you write it down so it never repeats again.

/retro-patterns: groups repeated complaints across sprints, not just the last one. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The AI groups. The team decides what action to take.

The Talent Journey

In Nerdbuster, teams were rigid.

Job requisitions came with fixed profiles, based on effort estimations.

"We need a junior Java programmer." That was all you knew.

You interviewed with a written exam and an algorithm on the whiteboard. That tested memory, not judgment.

Dynamic programming questions that nobody, the interviewer included, ever used on the job.

Onboarding meant two months of theory before touching the code.

"Read these courses, mark them done, fill in the forms. Then we'll see."

Offboarding was an HR formality: a form, an email, and the knowledge walking out the door.

In Nerdflix, it's a single journey.

Teams are flexible and built around talent and timing.

You find which skills are missing and look for those profiles inside or outside the company.

You interview with a fluent conversation and an ambiguous scenario.

You tell the candidate up front: "You'll be recorded. The AI and I will evaluate you."

The AI takes the notes and evaluates tone and English proficiency.

The candidate uses AI for the technical part. You evaluate their judgment and how they supervise the AI.

/match-positions-to-skills: builds flexible teams based on talent. 🧩

New people are productive from day one.

The senior keeps the judgment calls.

When someone leaves, you audit agents, skills, and the company brain, not just the laptop.

/code-review, /spec-review, /process-evaluation: make new people productive from day one. 🧩

You also guide the newcomer with a flexible journey:

/junior-mentor: supports juniors while the senior keeps the judgment calls. 🧩

Letting someone go is also part of the journey:

/offboarding-audit: revokes access to agents, skills, and the company brain. 🧩

⚠️ Bias: You supervise the AI for bias in every hiring step.

⚠️ Law: You get advice on your local labor laws.

🧭 Human in the loop: The team decides who gets hired, not a score. Onboarding includes mentoring and review.

Team Health and Individual Feedback

In Nerdbuster, you detected overload when deliveries were already failing. Too late.

Burnout management was reactive and based on gut feeling.

Feedback happened once a year, in a performance review tied to the bonus.

You used the feedback sandwich 🥪 and other recipes.

In Nerdflix, aggregated team patterns, like working hours and commits, suggest a conversation.

Never the detail of a single person.

The AI warns you: "Commits are consistently happening outside working hours."

You don't surveil anyone. You spot a burnout pattern.

You also read patterns in the ceremonies and in one-on-ones with AI transcripts.

Feedback is constant, in small doses.

The AI captures situational notes, so you avoid recency bias in the performance review.

/one-on-ones: prepares and records your one-on-ones. 🧩

A review that looks only at the last month is always unfair.

With notes, you can say: "In March, this didn't go well. Two months later, I saw you learned it."

It shows people that you pay attention.

You take the notes when things happen. Looking back, the traces are hard to find.

/journaling: takes notes in every meeting. 🧩

⚠️ Team signal, not individual surveillance: You look at team patterns, never at one person's activity.

⚠️ Consent: Transcribing or recording always requires consent.

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager gives the feedback. The AI detects signals. It doesn't diagnose people.

AI as a Sparring Partner for Difficult Conversations

In Nerdbuster, you rehearsed for five minutes in the hallway, or you just walked in.

You imagined the other person's reaction by projecting your own logic.

The difficult conversation was a Taylorist asymmetry: you informed, you didn't talk.

In Nerdflix, you practice with the AI in two directions.

First, the AI plays the difficult counterpart, so you rehearse your answers before the real conversation. It shows you where the person may get defensive.

Then, "Act as...": the AI becomes that person, so you understand their logic before you talk to them.

Regular one-on-ones use open questions, always practiced with the AI first.

You lean on the AI to think before you act.

Like this talk, actually.

🧭 Human in the loop: What to say and how to act is the person's decision.

Professional Development: Evaluate, Correct, Plan

In Nerdbuster, the evaluation was a generic form, unrelated to the actual role.

The improvement plan was an HR formality, the last step before firing someone, with no follow-up.

The career plan was arbitrary. Seniority or performance?

In Nerdflix, it's a single flow.

You evaluate against a competency specification by role and seniority, with evidence: pull requests, incidents, design decisions, and one-on-one notes.

"You're here. The next step needs you there. This is the gap."

/compare-competencies: compares the evidence against the role specification. 🧩

You don't talk in abstract terms like "work on your autonomy".

You point to the specific case where autonomy was missing.

The process improvement plan comes directly from the review gap. It's real support.

The career plan maps possible transitions against the missing competencies.

/weekly-check-ins: follows the improvement plan week by week. 🧩

Promotions are also part of the people journey:

/promotion-gap: maps career transitions against the missing competencies. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The manager runs the evaluation and the conversation. Extending, closing, or ending an improvement plan is decided together with Talent. The manager builds the career plan together with the person.

Salaries

In Nerdbuster, salaries were an arbitrary one-on-one negotiation.

How much you asked. How much the company dared to offer. How well you negotiated.

No market data.

Hallway gossip about who earns what was the closest thing to a salary survey.

Salary inequity, naturally.

In Nerdflix, you look at the sysarmy salary survey.

You compare the profile against a real market sample.

You calibrate. You don't guess.

/calibrate-role: calibrates the salary band for the role. 🧩

You do it all the time, because the market moves.

You might learn someone is unhappy this month because the market pays more.

/salary-benchmark: compares the profile against the market. 🧩

🧭 Human in the loop: The company makes the final call on the salary band, with the manager's calibration.

Other People Topics

I left out other big topics on the people side:

  • AI usage governance
  • Remote team rituals and culture
  • Diversity and inclusion
  • Peer conflicts
  • Wellness
  • Peer mentoring and coaching
  • Budget and contractor or vendor management

Please write new topic ideas for a third article in the comments.

The Manager's Territory

Managers added value by coordinating people.

With five, ten, or twenty people, the problem was always the same: you couldn't be everywhere.

Meetings, reports, dashboards, and objectives and key results (OKRs) all solved the same problem.

The real limitation was always the manager's cognitive capacity.

Now there's a machine that reads, summarizes, compares, and challenges decisions.

That goes beyond automating administrative tasks.

It's entering the manager's territory.

Human judgment is the most important thing.

That's why they hire you.

The AI doesn't have human judgment.

For now.

Automate, Operate, Augment

There are three levels of AI use:

  1. Automate: the AI does a task on its own.
  2. Operate: the AI runs a workflow or a sequence of tasks.
  3. Augment: the AI dramatically improves your ability to decide.

Image by boundsmarnie from Pixabay

This article is mostly about the third level.

That level separates the chatbot that summarizes your email from the AI that challenges your management decisions.

You shouldn't stay at the first or second level. You need to be augmented.

People ask me where to download my skills.

You can't. You build your own. They're personal.

You start by asking the AI: "Create a skill for me." Then you use it, refine it, and let it mature.

You build all these 🧩 skills by interacting with the AI, and you script the repeatable steps.

You can take these three concepts back to work.

Nobody Taught You

Managers aren't early adopters.

But you're as replaceable as any other role.

I didn't show you any specific tool.

This isn't theory. You can apply it right now.

I'd rather leave you with the itch.

You keep hearing that "AI won't replace you".

That's true.

But a manager who uses it well will.

It's not your fault. Nobody taught you.

Not your university, not your company, not YouTube.

Today, that changes.

articles.title: A Google 401, a Saved Connection, and the Wrong Reconnect Prompt
articles.description: In October 2026, a customer reported a specific interruption in Netsujo SIGNAL: after signing in...
articles.body_html:
In October 2026, a customer reported a specific interruption in Netsujo SIGNAL: after signing in again, the application kept asking them to reconnect Google.

For a product that reads Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Search Console data, that prompt can stop the user's real work. We took responsibility for investigating the behavior in our own software.

A crucial detail: the prompt was a symptom, not proof of a revoked OAuth grant.

We found three code paths that could lead to misleading reconnection guidance. We corrected them and tested the user journey on an authorized production workspace. We did not establish which one caused each occurrence in the original customer's environment, and we cannot infer an improvement in overall retention or revenue from this incident alone.

We mapped five different states

A single “connected / not connected” boolean is tempting. It hides distinct operating conditions.

Layer Question Evidence to inspect
Application session Can this user sign in to SIGNAL? Application session state
Google grant Does an existing authorization still apply? Stored grant and explicit revocation/refresh errors
Resource selection Which GA4 property or Search Console site is selected? Saved selection, resource availability, permissions
API read Can the selected resource be read now? Scoped Google API response and error class
Product workflow Can the user return to their analysis? A real browser journey and data readback

These layers suggest different next actions. A user with a valid Google connection but no selected GA4 property needs to choose a property—not repeat OAuth. An ambiguous API error needs diagnosis rather than an automatic “grant revoked” claim.

Three code-level corrections

1. An ordinary Google API 401 was classified too broadly. A generic HTTP 401 in a data-read path does not, by itself, establish the specific invalid_grant condition. We separated general authentication failures, token-related conditions, and explicit grant invalidation. This preserved reconnection guidance for genuine cases while removing an overly broad path to it.

2. A stored connection and unavailable resources had been conflated. The application could tell a returning user to perform first-time setup when a saved connection existed but no resource was currently readable. We separated the saved-connection state from the resource/readability state.

3. An unselected data source looked like an unconnected account. An existing Google connection with no GA4 property or Search Console site selected should present a selection step. We updated the relevant guidance to reflect that state.

These were targeted fixes; they did not require broadening a user's access to Google resources.

A small acceptance matrix

We use the following as a generalized regression design, not a literal export of our production tests:

Synthetic setup Correct behavior
Connected account; no property selected Show selection, preserve connection
Saved connection; insufficient permission for selected resource Explain access issue, avoid “first connection” label
Generic Google data API 401 with unknown root cause Report the scoped error; do not silently mark grant revoked
Explicit invalid grant Guide an authorized reconnection
Successful logout, login, and data read Preserve prior selection and display fresh accessible data

The critical test is whether the product gives the next correct action. A technically valid token and a useful screen are different results.

What we verified in production

On October 21, 2026, after the fixes were released, we used an authorized production workspace. We checked the saved GA4 and Search Console selections before logout, signed out, signed in through the normal owner-controlled flow, reloaded the relevant screens, and read both data sources again. We also checked another tab within the same browser session.

In that scope, the connection and data retrieval persisted without a forced Google reconnection. Our record covers our own workspace and browser session. It does not claim an independent repeat in the reporting customer's account, nor validation in an isolated browser profile.

That difference matters when someone writes “fixed” in a release note. Source checks, automated tests, deployment, and actual user-workflow acceptance are separate pieces of evidence.

What we carry into FDE engagements

Forward Deployed Engineering puts technical work close to a user's operating problem. For integrations, our practical sequence is:

  1. Record the exact interrupted user action and the last known good state.
  2. Identify each system boundary capable of producing the same visible symptom.
  3. Define the expected next action for every meaningful state, including unknowns.
  4. Make the narrowest correction that preserves permission boundaries.
  5. Validate through an authorized end-to-end user journey and say exactly where the evidence stops.

We apply this approach to our product work and to integrations where clients need the software to remain usable after release.

If a customer reports “the integration is disconnected,” which concrete state does your application verify before showing that message?

Our full first-party incident record contains the broader chronology and validation limits. Netsujo works on AI/SaaS integration, implementation, and production-use verification.

Disclosure: this is Netsujo's first-party incident report, not an external reproduction or a measurement of business impact. No customer identity, credentials, or raw production logs are published.

articles.title: I capped my game's streak bonus at 1.5x. Here's the math on breaking a streak.
articles.description: The most dangerous day in any streak isn't day 1. It's the day after you break it.  You miss one...
articles.body_html:
The most dangerous day in any streak isn't day 1. It's the day after you break it.

You miss one evening. The counter goes from 23 back to 0. And some quiet voice says: well, that's ruined, might as well take the week off.

I've felt that voice. If you've ever done #100DaysOfCode, you probably have too.

So when I was designing the daily rewards for Vigilante (my free browser game where real GitHub pushes open the next day of a 3D survival story), I had one question that took longer than any of the 3D code:

How big should the streak bonus get?

The answer I shipped is small and a bit boring: the daily supply crate gets x1.2 at 3 days and x1.5 at 7+ days. And then it stops growing. Forever.

That sounds like a weak reward. Here's why I think it's the right one, with the numbers.

The usual advice: make long streaks feel huge

Most streak systems scale with the streak. The longer you go, the bigger the bonus, because you want people to feel the weight of what they've built.

That works great right up until the streak breaks. Then the same weight lands on your foot.

Let's compare three ways to scale a reward. This is a simplified sketch to show the shape of the curves, not the production code:

// Three ways to scale a daily reward by streak length.
// Simplified sketch for this post, not Vigilante's real code.

const linear = (streak: number) => 1 + 0.1 * streak;          // +10% per day, no cap

const doubling = (streak: number) => Math.pow(2, Math.floor(streak / 7)); // doubles every week

const capped = (streak: number) => {
  if (streak >= 7) return 1.5;
  if (streak >= 3) return 1.2;
  return 1.0;
};

Now the question that matters: what does a break cost you? When a streak breaks, the multiplier falls back to 1.0. So the loss is how much of your daily reward vanishes overnight:

const lossOnBreak = (scale: (s: number) => number, streak: number) =>
  1 - 1 / scale(streak);

for (const s of [7, 14, 30]) {
  console.log(s,
    lossOnBreak(linear, s).toFixed(2),
    lossOnBreak(doubling, s).toFixed(2),
    lossOnBreak(capped, s).toFixed(2));
}

Run that and you get:

Streak broken at Linear (+10%/day) Doubling weekly Capped (x1.5)
Day 7 41% 50% 33%
Day 14 58% 75% 33%
Day 30 75% 94% 33%

Read the last row slowly.

With the "make it feel huge" curves, the person who showed up for 30 days straight is the one who gets punished hardest for one bad evening. With a doubling curve, they lose 94% of their reward. The most loyal player takes the biggest hit.

With the cap, a break always costs the same 33%. Day 7 or day 300, missing a day stings exactly as much. Not more.

Why "not more" matters

Think of a cricket batter on 94. The crowd is quiet. Every ball feels like it could end everything. Cricket even has a name for it: the nervous nineties.

An uncapped streak turns every day after day 30 into batting on 94.

I don't want someone's side project to feel like that. I want day 41 to feel like day 8: show up, push something real, open the crate, go to sleep.

The cap also kills a second problem. When the bonus keeps growing, the bonus becomes the reason you code. With a cap, after a week the crate stops getting bigger. The only thing still growing is the project. That's the thing I actually want to grow.

What a "day" has to be for any of this to work

A gentle reward system only works if the days are real. Otherwise people (me included, on a tired night) will just feed it junk.

So a day in Vigilante is only verified from real GitHub push data, and some commits are filtered out on purpose: merge commits, empty commits, and commits that only touch lock files or config. The game never reads the code itself, only commit IDs, timestamps and file names.

That's the deal: the reward is gentle, the definition of a day is strict.

The other two rules I keep coming back to

Capping the bonus was one decision. Two others came from the same thinking.

1. A repaired day is not a verified day.

There's an item called Revival Fluid that repairs a missed day so the story can continue. But it never counts as verified. Your share card and your record still show the truth. I'd rather the game forgive you than lie for you.

2. Money never opens a day.

There are optional purchases, but buying anything never opens a story day or counts as verified work. If money could buy a day, the streak would stop meaning "I showed up." It would mean "I paid."

Both of these are the same idea as the cap: protect what the streak means, and keep the pain of a bad day small.

If you're building any kind of streak

Here's the short version I wish I'd had before starting:

  • Calculate the loss on break, not just the reward. Run lossOnBreak for day 30 before you ship any curve. If the number scares you, it'll scare your users more.
  • Cap early. A week is long enough to build a habit worth rewarding. After that, the reward should be the work itself.
  • Be strict about what counts. Gentle rewards plus loose rules equals a streak full of empty commits.
  • Let people recover, but never fake the record. Repairs keep someone in the game. Honest records keep the game worth playing.

None of this is new psychology. It's mostly just refusing to punish the people who stayed the longest.

If you want to see how it feels in practice, the GitHub streak tracker is free and Day 1 of the game needs no sign-up. Full disclosure: I built it, nights and weekends, around a Java day job.

What's the longest streak you've ever broken, and what did you do the next day?

articles.title: Could I Still Do This From Scratch?
articles.description: The thing that every dev I know is quietly worrying about is not AI taking their job. It's losing the...
articles.body_html:
The thing that every dev I know is quietly worrying about is not AI taking their job. It's losing the skill to do their job.

We're not talking about it out loud because it feels like admitting weakness, and because these tools are genuinely powerful. You can roll out a feature in an afternoon that previously took you a week. Autocomplete guesses what you're thinking. A chat agent lets you restructure that flaky module you've been avoiding for months. But then in that in-between moment, the third or fourth prompt, the third or fourth tab-tab-tab-accept cycle, that quiet question pops up: could I still do this from scratch?

Now don't get me wrong, I'm not saying that devs couldn't write a for loop if they wanted to. I'm saying that this part is what's fading. The deep work of wrestling with a problem, thinking it through, fumbling around in the dark until the solution crystallizes. Because instead of spending fifteen minutes thinking through the problem, the model gives you the answer in fifteen seconds, so what you're doing is no longer building something. You're reviewing it, which is a far less taxing and less creative task.

The research is starting to catch up with this concern. In a Microsoft study presented at CHI 2025, 319 knowledge workers showed a clear trend: the higher the trust in AI-generated content, the lower the level of critical thinking. The change in workflow is not about problem solving, but about checking and integrating. In another study, this time from MIT Media Lab about essay writing, people who used LLMs were the ones with the worst brain connectivity. They called it cognitive debt. Even productivity is more doubtful than the hype says: in a 2025 study by METR, experienced open source developers using AI tools turned out to be slower than those who didn't, but convinced themselves of the opposite.

All the devs I know have felt this, not as some abstract fear, but as a concrete experience of reaching for an answer and realizing the shelf is empty. I don't need a study to tell me that the knowledge I used to have is slipping away. That the syntax I once produced on autopilot is now a few keystrokes and a prompt away. That the kind of instinct only a developer who's been through dozens of bad architectural decisions can have is now being outsourced to a model that has seen a million architectures but never lived inside one.

The scary part is that it happens under the radar. You're still writing good code, because the model writes good code. You're still getting good performance reviews. You're still shipping. Until you're not, and that's when the tools don't work: when a weird bug shows up, when a novel constraint hits, when an edge case the training data never saw appears. Only then do you realize if there's actually a developer under the hood, or if it's just a workflow.

No one wants to go back to the old days of writing boilerplate the hard way. But the devs who are quietly preparing are doing it in the not-so-cool way: writing some code without AI, wrestling through the confusion, keeping those weak muscles working. The scary part is not that AI will replace you. It's that one day you'll wake up and you'll have replaced yourself, one accepted suggestion at a time.

articles.title: Git 2.56's git add --resolved only checks conflict markers while git still calls a file unmerged
articles.description: I tested Git 2.56's new add --resolved flag: it kept an unrelated edit out of a merge commit, but its conflict-marker check stopped working the moment the index stopped calling a file unmerged.
articles.body_html:
Git 2.56 shipped a new flag for the oldest bad habit in merge conflict resolution: typing git add . the moment the markers are gone, and staging whatever else happened to be sitting in the working tree at the same time.

git add --resolved is supposed to fix that. It stages only the paths git still considers unmerged, and it is meant to refuse if any of those paths still contain leftover conflict markers. I built it from source, because the Ubuntu 24.04 container I was working in only had 2.43.0, and ran it against a handful of conflicts I created on purpose.

The core promise held up. The safety check around it had a gap I didn't expect.

Setting it up

Git 2.56.0 isn't in Ubuntu's repositories yet, so I built it from the kernel.org tarball:

$ ./configure --prefix=$HOME/git-2.56
$ make -j4 NO_GETTEXT=1 NO_TCLTK=1 NO_CURL=1
$ make install NO_GETTEXT=1 NO_TCLTK=1 NO_CURL=1
$ ./git-2.56/bin/git --version
git version 2.56.0

I skipped curl and gettext support because the testing only needed local commands. git add -h confirmed the flag is there:

    --[no-]resolved       add conflict-resolved tracked files

The core promise: it does ignore unrelated files

I built a repo with two branches that both edit file1.txt and file2.txt, merged them to force a conflict, resolved both files properly, and then made an unrelated edit to a third file, file4.txt, that had nothing to do with the merge.

Command file1.txt (resolved) file2.txt (resolved) file4.txt (unrelated edit)
git add . staged staged staged
git add --resolved . staged staged left unstaged

That's the whole pitch, and it's real. After git add --resolved ., git status --short showed:

M  file1.txt
M  file2.txt
 M file4.txt

The leading column is the staged state and the second is the working-tree state. file4.txt has a space in the first column, meaning nothing about it is staged. With plain git add . on the same working tree, all three files come back M in the index column. If you've ever committed a stray console.log or a half-finished change because it happened to be sitting in the tree during a conflict resolution, this removes that failure mode outright.

What it refuses, and what I got wrong on the way

The second claim is that --resolved checks the paths it's about to stage for leftover <<<<<<< markers and aborts if it finds any. My first attempt to test this looked like it had found a bug: I resolved one file, left markers in the other on purpose, ran the command, and got exit code 0 with nothing printed and nothing staged.

That looked like a silent no-op where the documentation promised an error. It wasn't. The problem was my test harness, not the flag. In the run before that one, I had already run git add --resolved . successfully once on that same working tree and then called git reset to put things back for the next scenario. git reset rewrites the index against HEAD, and in doing so it collapses the unmerged (stage 1/2/3) entries into ordinary staged-then-unstaged entries. By the time I reintroduced the markers, git no longer considered those paths unmerged at all, so --resolved had nothing to look at and correctly did nothing. I was testing a file that looked conflicted to a human and wasn't conflicted to git.

Once I rebuilt the conflict from scratch instead of reusing a reset repo, the refusal showed up exactly as documented:

$ git add --resolved .
fatal: the following paths still have conflict markers:
    file2.txt

Exit code 128. And it's atomic: file1.txt was fully and correctly resolved in that same run, but it stayed UU in the index alongside the broken file2.txt. --resolved does not partially stage the paths it's happy with; one bad file blocks the whole invocation. Only after I actually removed the markers from file2.txt did the second run stage both files.

The gap: the check only applies while git calls a file unmerged

The accidental discovery above pointed at something real, so I tested it on purpose. I merged two branches with one conflicting file, left the file with genuine, un-removed <<<<<<< markers, and ran git add --resolved -v . against it while there was no merge in progress and no unmerged entry for that path at all — just an ordinary tracked file with marker text sitting inside it from an earlier git reset.

$ git status --short
 M file1.txt
$ git add --resolved -v .
$ echo exit: $?
exit: 0

No output, even with -v. Nothing staged. The file still contains real <<<<<<< and ======= and >>>>>>> lines, and --resolved walked straight past it, because the only thing it checks is whether the path is in conflict stages in the index right now, not whether the file's content looks like a conflict. The marker scan is a guard on top of "this file is still unmerged," not a general scan for marker text in tracked files. If you've already run any add/reset sequence that clears the unmerged bit — including, ironically, a first successful use of --resolved itself followed by amending something — the safety net is gone and the next --resolved call will happily do nothing, silently, on a file that still has markers in it.

The other gap: it doesn't look inside a file

I then resolved a conflict and, in the same edit, added one extra unrelated line to the same file, to see whether --resolved could tell the two apart:

 line1
 main change
+A change
+UNRELATED DEBUG LINE I FORGOT TO REMOVE

git add --resolved . staged this without complaint. The flag's unit of "unrelated" is the file, not the line. It stops you from staging file4.txt because it's a different path. It will not stop you from staging a debug line you left in the middle of the file you were actually supposed to be fixing.

What it costs

I timed git add --resolved . against plain git add . on a repo with 3,000 genuinely conflicting files, all pre-resolved, five runs each:

Run add --resolved add
1 0.202s 0.196s
2 0.223s 1.404s
3 0.202s 0.230s
4 0.439s 0.168s
5 0.820s 0.175s

The spread swamps the difference. I expected scanning every conflicted file's content for marker strings to show up as a consistent tax on top of ordinary staging, and it didn't: the two distributions overlap, and the single slowest run in the whole table (1.4s) belongs to plain add, not --resolved. On this machine, at this scale, the marker check is not a cost worth worrying about.

Run it yourself 

#!/bin/bash
set -e
GIT=/path/to/git-2.56/bin/git
$GIT init -q -b main repo && cd repo
$GIT config user.email t@t.com && $GIT config user.name T
echo base > a.txt; echo base > b.txt
$GIT add . && $GIT commit -q -m base
$GIT checkout -q -b branchA
echo "A change" >> a.txt; echo "A change" >> b.txt
$GIT commit -q -am branchA
$GIT checkout -q main
echo "main change" >> a.txt; echo "main change" >> b.txt
echo "unrelated edit" >> c.txt
$GIT commit -q -am main
set +e
$GIT merge branchA  # conflicts in a.txt and b.txt
set -e

# resolve a.txt and b.txt by hand:
printf "base\nmain change\nA change\n" > a.txt
printf "base\nmain change\nA change\n" > b.txt

$GIT add --resolved .
$GIT status --short   # c.txt stays unstaged

I ran this exact sequence while writing the post and it produces the table above.

What to do with this

If your merge workflow still ends in git add ., switching to git add --resolved removes a real failure mode: unrelated dirty files no longer ride along into the merge commit, for free, with no measurable cost. Don't treat the marker check as a general-purpose guard against committing broken conflict markers, though. It only fires while git's index still thinks the path is unmerged. If you've run any sequence that clears that state — a reset, an aborted add, a rebase that re-touches the same path — check the file yourself before you commit, because --resolved will not catch it, and it will not tell you it didn't.
