articles.title: Reflektor - Code review on steroids
articles.description: Check it out on GitHub: github.com/bashovski/reflektor           A little rant, and why I built...
articles.body_html:
Check it out on GitHub: github.com/bashovski/reflektor

A little rant, and why I built Reflektor

Microsoft went down the other day, and it took them a long time to get back up. The question is, do they even have any developers at the firm who actually know how things work?

Now it's just prompting LLMs and praying that they'll find the issue.

Code gets pushed blindly. We lowered the bar so we can ship faster.

You used to write every single line of code, and you knew what it did. Now, you have no clue.

Devs ask other devs to review their PRs without looking at a single line of code themselves. Guilty yet?

This is nothing new, but how does one protect their codebase from AI slop and actually have some ownership?

I held onto an idea of a high-level, quality PR report for a long time, until I made it this week and released it.

Reflektor.

It's built with short review times in mind and oriented towards the direction a PR is taking, rather than focusing on variable names.

While thinking of where reviewers would save the most time, a few things came to mind:

  • Being able to see the actual UI that's new or has been changed
  • Knowing what to review and what to skim
  • Being aware of the Database model/schema changes
  • Looking for new types, interfaces, etc.
  • Knowing any risks before a PR goes live

Do I need to know every single line of code?

  • No. Do I need to know whether your PR ships 1,000 lines of slop, or is it a meaningful PR? - Yes!

What's released, and what's to come

In the initial release that went live just this morning, a skill that you can run yourself in any codebase is fully ready and tested on all major agents, and it works.

The skill is tech-agnostic, meaning it's working with any tech stack you throw its way. When you invoke/run a skill, it runs a daemon in the background and it additionally augments your reports and strengthens your Developer Experience, while everything runs locally.

Optionally, you can connect to reflektor.dev and push reports automatically to the platform and have your teammates review them.

Feel free to run as many verification/review loops, because that's what is gonna turn any PR into a good PR.

Get Started

To get started, I'd strongly advise you to open the GitHub Repo or the Install Page and run the skill on one of your sessions.

You can simply install the skill:

npx skills add bashovski/reflektor#skill -g

and then run:

/reflektor

It's the best way to get started, and you'd save time having to read every single line of code. AI doesn't optimize code generation for readability by default. So, additionally, you may want to tweak your AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md further to do so.

List of features

  • Technology-agnostic
  • Review Loops
  • Collaboration
  • Automatic Project Checks
  • E2E UI Testing with Screenshots
  • Flow Visualizations
  • Database Changes Visualizations
  • Test Coverage Summaries and Reports
  • Hooks (allows pipelines customization)
  • Daemon (runs in background)

articles.title: AI Invented This npm Package. Someone Registered It. (Slopsquatting)
articles.description: Your AI assistant tells you to install a package. The name sounds right, but the package doesn't...
articles.body_html:
Your AI assistant tells you to install a package. The name sounds right, but the package doesn't exist: the AI made it up. If an attacker registers that name first, the next npm install runs their code.

This attack is called slopsquatting. Here's a real case, a harmless demo of why installing alone is enough, and a 10-second check you can run before installing anything an AI suggests.

All registry numbers below were checked live on November 15, 2026.

Video version:

How slopsquatting works

  1. An AI model suggests a package name that doesn't exist. It sounds plausible, often a mix of two real names.
  2. Different models (and the same model, asked again) often invent the same fake names. Researchers have measured this across several frontier models, so the names are predictable.
  3. An attacker collects those names and publishes real packages under them, with malware inside.
  4. The next developer, or AI agent, who follows the suggestion installs it.

A name-similarity scanner won't help much here. The fake name isn't a typo of a real package; it's a brand-new name.

A real case: react-codeshift

AI-generated agent instructions ("skills") told people to run:

npx react-codeshift …

That command ended up in 200+ files on GitHub. But react-codeshift never existed. The AI had blended two real packages: jscodeshift (Facebook's codemod runner) and react-codemod (the React team's transforms).

On January 14, 2026, Charlie Eriksen, a security researcher at Aikido, noticed and registered the name first, as a harmless placeholder:

$ npm view react-codeshift description
🚫 Placeholder to prevent dependency confusion.

It's still downloaded about 31 times a week (59 times in the last month), most likely by agents and people following those instructions. If an attacker had claimed it first, every one of those installs would have run their code.

Installing is enough: postinstall

You don't even have to import a malicious package. npm runs lifecycle scripts such as postinstall automatically during npm install:

{
  "name": "evil-demo",
  "version": "1.0.1",
  "scripts": {
    "postinstall": "node -e \"require('fs').writeFileSync(require('os').tmpdir()+'/pwned-demo.txt','x')\""
  }
}

I packed that harmless demo package and installed it with npm 11.4:

  • npm install ./evil-demo-1.0.1.tgz: the output showed only added 1 package, but the marker file was created. The script ran silently, with full access to my environment variables (77 of them; a version that printed Object.keys(process.env).length showed it).
  • npm install ./evil-demo-1.0.1.tgz --ignore-scripts: no marker file. The script never ran.

A real attack would read ~/.npmrc, .env files, SSH keys or cloud tokens instead of writing a marker file.

The 10-second check

Before installing something an AI suggests, ask the registry three questions: does it exist, how old is it, and does anyone use it?

// check-pkg.mjs (Node 18+)
const name = process.argv[2];
const reg = "https://registry.npmjs.org/";
const res = await fetch(reg + name);
if (res.status === 404) {
  console.log(`❌ ${name}: does not exist`); process.exit(1);
}
const { time } = await res.json();
const days = Math.round((Date.now() - new Date(time.created)) / 864e5);
const api = "https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/";
const { downloads } = await (await fetch(api + name)).json();
console.log(`${name}: ${days} days old, ${downloads.toLocaleString("en-US")} downloads/week`);

$ node check-pkg.mjs jscodeshift
jscodeshift: 4254 days old, 7,656,282 downloads/week
$ node check-pkg.mjs react-codeshift
react-codeshift: 305 days old, 31 downloads/week
$ node check-pkg.mjs express-jwt-validator-pro
❌ express-jwt-validator-pro: does not exist
  • The real package is over 11 years old with 7.6 million downloads a week.
  • The hallucinated one is new and almost unused.
  • A name that doesn't exist at all is the clearest red flag. Don't install it, and don't "fix" it by registering it yourself. Find the real package.

New and unpopular doesn't always mean malicious, but it does mean "look closer": check the repository link, the maintainers and what the code actually does.

For Python, the same check is pip index versions <name> (No matching distribution found means it doesn't exist) or https://pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json (a 404 means the same).

Checklist: before you install what AI suggests

  • ✅ Check that it exists, its age, its weekly downloads and its repository.
  • ✅ Prefer packages you already know, or the ones named in the official docs.
  • ⚠️ Be suspicious of names that look like a mashup of two real packages.
  • ✅ Review new dependencies in pull requests, including the ones an agent added.
  • ✅ Don't let AI agents install packages without approval.
  • ✅ Use npm install --ignore-scripts (or ignore-scripts=true in .npmrc) when you can. Some packages genuinely need install scripts, so test that your project still builds.

Has an AI ever suggested a package to you that didn't exist? 👇

I post one tested coding tip every day on YouTube at Refactorly. The 30-second version of this one is here.

articles.title: I said my MJML i18n library would never have loops. Then we needed a list.
articles.description: Back in May I wrote about @checkthiscloud/mjml-i18n, a tiny MJML preprocessor that gives your email...
articles.body_html:
Back in May I wrote about @checkthiscloud/mjml-i18n, a tiny MJML preprocessor that gives your email templates exactly two things: variables and co-located translations. I was pretty proud of what it didn't do:

No loops, no conditionals, no arbitrary expressions, no eval. […] That constraint is the whole point.

Version 0.1 adds loops and conditionals.

So yeah — we changed our mind. Here's why, and where the line still holds.

What broke the rule: a daily digest

The two-tiny-things model is perfect for transactional email: "Hi {name}, here's your link." One template, a handful of values, done.

Then we needed a daily digest. You know the shape:

  • a headline with today's count — or a calm "nothing urgent" message when there's nothing,
  • one row per item, each with a link and an optional note,
  • a schedule grouped by day, with a nested list of events under each day.

None of that is two tiny things. It's a list, an empty state, an optional field and a list inside a list.

Without loops in the template, you have exactly two options, and both are bad:

  1. Build the HTML in code and pass it in as a variable. Now your markup lives in a JS string, outside MJML, and you've lost the whole reason you're using MJML.
  2. Go back to running a full template engine before MJML. Which is literally the thing this library exists to avoid.

We stopped pretending a list was an edge case.

What it looks like now

Same {{ … }} markers, a few new statement shapes:

<mjml>
  <i18n type="json">
    {
      "en": { "title": "Today: {count} items", "calm": "Nothing urgent", "guests": "{count} guests", "open": "Open" },
      "cs": { "title": "Počet úkolů dnes: {count}", "calm": "Nic nehoří", "guests": "{count} hostů", "open": "Otevřít" }
    }
  </i18n>
  <mj-body>
    <mj-section><mj-column>
      {{ if items }}
      <mj-text>{{ i18n('title', { count: get('itemCount') }) }}</mj-text>
      {{ else }}
      <mj-text>{{ i18n('calm') }}</mj-text>
      {{ endif }}
    </mj-column></mj-section>

    {{ for item in items }}
    <mj-section><mj-column>
      <mj-text>{{ get('item.title') }}</mj-text>
      {{ if item.note }}<mj-text>{{ get('item.note') }}</mj-text>{{ endif }}
      <mj-button href="{{ get('item.url') }}">{{ i18n('open') }}</mj-button>
    </mj-column></mj-section>
    {{ endfor }}

    {{ for day in days }}
    <mj-section><mj-column>
      <mj-text>{{ get('day.label') }}</mj-text>
      <mj-table>
        {{ for event in day.events }}
        <tr><td>{{ get('event.name') }}</td><td>{{ i18n('guests', { count: get('event.guests') }) }}</td></tr>
        {{ endfor }}
      </mj-table>
    </mj-column></mj-section>
    {{ endfor }}
  </mj-body>
</mjml>

Rendering hasn't changed:

import mjml from 'mjml';
import { createI18nPreprocessor } from '@checkthiscloud/mjml-i18n';

const preprocessor = createI18nPreprocessor({
  locale: 'cs',
  vars: {
    itemCount: 2,
    items: [
      { title: 'Approve the reminder', note: 'Due at 9:00', url: 'https://example.com/a' },
      { title: 'Check the domain', note: null, url: 'https://example.com/b' },
    ],
    days: [
      { label: 'Saturday', events: [{ name: 'Fair', guests: 1900 }, { name: 'Ball', guests: 820 }] },
      { label: 'Sunday', events: [{ name: 'Run', guests: 2400 }] },
    ],
  },
});

const { html } = await mjml(template, { preprocessors: [preprocessor] });

The loop variable (item, day, event) works everywhere you'd expect it to: in get(), inside i18n() params and in nested blocks. Because the blocks are resolved on the raw XML before MJML parses it, a for can repeat a whole <mj-section> or just a <tr> inside an <mj-table> — MJML only ever sees the finished markup.

Where we kept the line

The new syntax is the smallest thing that makes the digest work. There is no expression language:

  • Conditions take a path, never an expression. {{ if item.note }} is fine. {{ if a && b }}, {{ if count > 0 }} and {{ if(a) }} are not statements at all — they get left in the output untouched, like any other marker the library doesn't recognize.
  • Want a comparison? Compute it in your data. Pass order.isLate, not order.dueAt < now. That logic belongs in code you can test, not in an email template.
  • Truthiness is boring on purpose. false, null, undefined, '', 0, NaN and an empty list are false; everything else is true. An empty list being false is what makes {{ if items }} … {{ else }} … {{ endif }} work as an empty state.
  • A loop variable owns its name. Inside {{ for item in items }}, a typo like get('item.titel') reports Missing variable: item.titel. It doesn't quietly fall through to some global called item.
  • Still no eval. The only statement shapes are for <name> in <path>, endfor, if <path>, else and endif; everything else goes through the same tiny allowlist evaluator as before.

So it's still not a template engine. It's loops and ifs over data you've already prepared.

The breaking change: get() now escapes

Once you loop over a list of things users typed in — titles, notes, names — you're putting user data into HTML and into attributes. So in 0.1, values read by get() are HTML-escaped: &, <, >, " and ' become entities.

<mj-text>{{ get('comment') }}</mj-text>
<!-- "<b>hi</b>" now prints as text, not as bold -->

Translations are part of your template, so their markup is kept. A get() value handed into i18n() params is escaped, so a translation like "Welcome <strong>{name}</strong>" keeps its <strong> but can't be broken by a name like Tom & <Jerry>.

If you were deliberately passing markup through vars, that's the part that changes for you. (And honestly: you shouldn't have been.)

One honest note: 0.1.0 printed Date objects as [object Object]. We missed that the deep escaping walked every object, including the ones that have their own string form. 0.1.1 fixes it — Dates, URLs and class instances print through String() again, escaped. Use 0.1.1 or newer.

Mistakes stay loud, not fatal

Same philosophy as before: nothing throws into your render. A broken template prints its problem right where it happened, so you see it in the preview instead of the render blowing up:

You wrote You get
{{ for x in missing }} Missing variable: missing
{{ for x in title }} (a string) Not a list: title
an endfor with nothing to close Unexpected endfor
a for you forgot to close Unclosed block: for item in items

That's great in a preview, less great when it lands in a customer's inbox.

What's still missing

Look at the Czech translation above: "{count} hostů". That's correct for 1900 guests. For 2 guests, Czech says 2 hosté; for 1, 1 host. Params are still plain {name} substitution, so plurals are on you for now. ICU message format is on the roadmap, and the formatting layer is already a swap-in seam, so it can land without touching the marker syntax.

Try it

It's 0.x, MIT, built for MJML v5.

npm install @checkthiscloud/mjml-i18n@^0.1.1 mjml
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@checkthiscloud/mjml-i18n
  • GitHub: https://github.com/CheckThisCloud/mjml-i18n

In May I said the constraint was the whole point. I still think it is — we just moved it. The rule used to be "no logic in templates". Now it's "no expressions in templates". That turned out to be the line that actually matters.

articles.title: Uploading a 5 GB video just to transcribe it? Extract the audio in the browser first
articles.description: If someone wants a transcript of a 2-hour screen recording, the file on their disk might be 4 GB. But...
articles.body_html:
If someone wants a transcript of a 2-hour screen recording, the file on their disk might be 4 GB. But the part a speech-to-text model needs is the sound, and speech models work at 16 kHz mono anyway. At 32 kbps Opus, an hour of mono speech is about 14 MB. Ten hours is about 144 MB.

So for TranscribeLink I stopped asking people to upload the video. The browser pulls the audio track out first and uploads only that. Here's how it works and what I had to get right.

The tools: WebCodecs + Mediabunny

WebCodecs gives the browser access to native audio encoders and decoders (AudioDecoder, AudioEncoder). On its own it doesn't read containers like MP4, MOV, MKV or WebM. For that I use Mediabunny, a small library that demuxes and muxes those formats in the browser and drives WebCodecs for you.

The core of it is a "conversion" that drops the video track and re-encodes the audio:

const input = new Input({ source: new BlobSource(file), formats: ALL_FORMATS });
if (!(await input.getPrimaryAudioTrack())) throw new Error('No audio track');

const output = new Output({ format: new OggOutputFormat(), target: new BufferTarget() });
const conversion = await Conversion.init({
  input, output,
  video: { discard: true },
  audio: { codec: 'opus', numberOfChannels: 1, sampleRate: 16000, bitrate: 32000, forceTranscode: true },
});
conversion.onProgress = (p) => showProgress(p);
await conversion.execute();

const audio = new File([output.target.buffer], 'audio.ogg', { type: 'audio/ogg' });

BlobSource reads the file in slices, so a 5 GB video never has to fit in memory.

Fallbacks matter more than the happy path

Not every browser can encode Opus. I try two targets in order and check each one first with canEncodeAudio:

  1. Opus, mono, 16 kHz, 32 kbps, in an Ogg file (about 14 MB an hour)
  2. AAC, mono, 44.1 kHz, 48 kbps, in an MP4 file (about 22 MB an hour)

If the browser has no AudioEncoder at all (older Safari), or neither codec works, nothing breaks: it just uploads the original file. Extraction is an optimisation, never a requirement.

Don't wait for extraction: race it

Extracting audio from a long file takes time, and on a fast connection the original might upload before extraction finishes. So both start at once:

  • The original file starts uploading in chunks right away.
  • Extraction runs in parallel.
  • When extraction finishes, compare: if the bytes still left to upload are more than the size of the extracted audio, stop the upload, tell the server to replace it, and send the audio instead. Otherwise cancel extraction and let the original finish. 
const first = await Promise.race([
  sending.then((result) => ({ sent: result })),
  extraction.promise.then((audio) => ({ audio }), (error) => ({ audio: null, error })),
]);

if (first.audio && file.size * (1 - uploadedFraction) > first.audio.size) {
  stopUpload();
  await replaceOnServer(first.audio.size);
  await upload(first.audio);
}

On a slow connection the audio almost always wins, and that's exactly where it saves the most time.

Small details that caught me

  • Resumed uploads keep the original. I resume interrupted uploads by byte offset. Extracted audio isn't byte-identical between runs, so a resumed upload continues with the original file instead of re-extracting.
  • Skip tiny files. Below about 1 MB, extraction isn't worth the overhead, so those go up as they are.
  • Load the library early. Mediabunny is about 690 KB minified. I start loading it when the user opens the file picker, so it's ready by the time they've chosen a file.
  • Use XMLHttpRequest for chunks. fetch doesn't report upload progress, so a big chunk shows 0% until it's done. xhr.upload.onprogress lets the progress bar move smoothly, which matters when people are watching a multi-GB upload.

Result

A long video becomes an audio file of tens of megabytes before it leaves the user's machine. The upload that used to be the slowest step is now usually the shortest, and the server never has to store or process the video.

I use this in TranscribeLink, where you can upload files up to 10 hours or 5 GB, or paste a video link, and get a transcript in 100 languages. If you've done something similar, I'd like to hear how you handled browsers without WebCodecs.

articles.title: How I keep bots out of my own analytics, with no cookies and no third-party scripts
articles.description: Five small checks that stop crawlers, headless browsers and scripts from inflating page views on a side project, in about 80 lines of code.
articles.body_html:
I run a small file converter, imageconvert.art. Like most side projects, I wanted to know one thing: are real people using it?

I didn't want Google Analytics (cookie banner, a third-party script on every page, data I don't need). So I wrote a tiny page-view counter of my own. On the first day it said I had visitors. Lots of them. Most of them, it turned out, weren't people.

Here's how I fixed it with five small checks. No cookies, no fingerprinting, nothing stored that identifies anyone.

The naive version

Count a view every time the server renders a page. That counts everything: Googlebot, Bingbot, uptime monitors, SEO crawlers, link previews from chat apps, and the random scanners that hit every new domain looking for /wp-login.php.

Moving the count to a JavaScript beacon fixes the simplest crawlers, because they never run JavaScript:

navigator.sendBeacon("/ui/v", JSON.stringify({ p: location.pathname, r: document.referrer }));

But plenty of bots do run JavaScript now: headless Chrome, preview renderers, and Google's own renderer. So I added more layers.

1. Only count a view after a real interaction

A person scrolls, moves the mouse, taps or presses a key. A headless browser that loads the page and leaves does none of that. And events a script fires itself have isTrusted === false, so they don't count either.

if (navigator.webdriver) return; // automated browsers announce themselves

const kinds = ["pointermove", "pointerdown", "touchstart", "wheel", "scroll", "keydown"];
let sent = false;
const onAct = (e) => {
  if (sent || !e.isTrusted || document.visibilityState !== "visible") return;
  sent = true;
  kinds.forEach((k) => removeEventListener(k, onAct, true));
  send();
};
kinds.forEach((k) => addEventListener(k, onAct, { capture: true, passive: true }));

This was the single biggest improvement. The trade-off: someone who opens a page and reads it without touching anything isn't counted. On a tool site where every visit involves clicking something, that's rare.

2. A signed token proves the page was really served

Anyone can POST to /ui/v. To make sure a ping came from a page my server actually rendered, every page carries a small signed timestamp:

<body data-vt="1763290000.3f9a1c...">

The beacon sends it back, and the server checks the signature (HMAC-SHA256 with a key that only exists in memory) and its age:

var age = now - DateTimeOffset.FromUnixTimeSeconds(secs);
return age >= TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1) && age <= TimeSpan.FromHours(12);

At least one second old means a script that fetches the page and fires the beacon instantly doesn't count. At most 12 hours means a token can't be harvested once and replayed forever. Because the key lives in memory, a restart invalidates old tokens; the cost is losing a few views, which I'm fine with.

3. Check Sec-Fetch-Site

Real browsers add a Sec-Fetch-Site header to every request. A beacon from my own page says same-origin. A request forged from another site says cross-site, so it's dropped:

var site = ctx.Request.Headers["Sec-Fetch-Site"].ToString();
if (site.Length > 0 && site != "same-origin") return;

(If the header is missing entirely, I let it through, since some older browsers don't send it.)

4. Cap views per visitor per day

No human views 60 pages of a file converter in one day. Past that, it's a script:

public const int MaxViewsPerVisitorPerDay = 60;
return _viewCounts.AddOrUpdate(hash, 1, (_, n) => n + 1) <= MaxViewsPerVisitorPerDay;

5. The usual user-agent list, and skip myself

Known bot user agents are dropped, and so are views from my own admin account, so testing doesn't inflate the numbers.

What about privacy?

To count unique visitors without cookies, I hash the IP address and user agent together with a random salt that changes every day and is never stored. The same person on the same day gets the same hash; tomorrow it's a different one, and nobody, me included, can turn a hash back into an IP. The raw IP is never saved.

Was it worth it?

The whole thing is about 80 lines across one C# class and one small script. What I got:

  • Numbers I actually believe, so I can tell whether a Reddit post or a new guide brought anyone.
  • No cookie banner, because nothing is stored in the visitor's browser.
  • No third-party script slowing down the page.

It won't stop a determined attacker who drives a real browser and fakes mouse movement. But nobody is doing that to inflate the stats of a side project. The goal is to filter out the everyday automated noise, and these five checks do that well.

If you want to see it running, the converter is at imageconvert.art. I'm happy to answer questions in the comments.

articles.title: Fifteen developer tools, zero dependencies
articles.description: A tour of the platform APIs behind 15 client-side developer tools: Web Crypto's gaps, OKLCH maths, cron next-run search, LCS diffing and JSON-to-TypeScript inference.
articles.body_html:
Fifteen developer tools, zero dependencies

Most "online JSON formatter" pages send your payload to a server, keep it for a while, and hope you don't think about it. Building tools that don't need to is mostly a matter of knowing which platform APIs already exist, and being willing to write the small amount of maths that a library would otherwise hide.

ryuslog.com/tools now has fifteen of them — JSON, YAML, diff, regex, SQL, CSV, JWT, Base64, URL, hash, cURL, UUID, timestamps, cron and colour/contrast. All of them run entirely in the tab: no upload, no account, no server round trip. This is what that actually takes, and where the sharp edges are.

The rule that shapes everything

Every tool is one pure function from input to output, with the DOM kept at the edges:

type ToolResult<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string; at?: number };

export function formatJson(input: string, opts: JsonOptions): ToolResult<string> { /* … */ }

That shape buys three things at once. The engine is testable without a browser, the UI is a thin shell that renders ToolResult, and an error carries a position so the editor can underline the offending character instead of saying "invalid input".

The rest is browser API archaeology.

Web Crypto: generous, with two gaps

crypto.subtle.digest covers SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, is fast, and returns an ArrayBuffer you hex-encode yourself:

async function sha256(text: string) {
  const buf = await crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(text));
  return [...new Uint8Array(buf)].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join('');
}

Two gaps matter for developer tooling:

  • MD5 is not there. Plenty of legacy checksums still need it, so the hash generator computes MD5 in plain TypeScript and uses subtle for the SHA family.
  • Nothing is timing-safe for you. Verifying an HMAC (as a JWT signature check would) is importKey + sign + a byte-wise comparison — === on hex strings leaks timing, and comparing base64url strings is worse because of padding.

There is also a third gap that trips people up: subtle is only available in a secure context, so the same code silently fails on http://192.168.x.x during development.

OKLCH in about forty lines

The colour tool converts HEX → RGB → HSL → OKLCH and back, and checks WCAG contrast. OKLCH is where the maths is:

const toLinear = (c: number) => (c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4);

// linear sRGB -> Oklab
const l = 0.4122214708 * r + 0.5363325363 * g + 0.0514459929 * b;
const m = 0.2119034982 * r + 0.6806995451 * g + 0.1073969566 * b;
const s = 0.0883024619 * r + 0.2817188376 * g + 0.6299787005 * b;

const l_ = Math.cbrt(l), m_ = Math.cbrt(m), s_ = Math.cbrt(s);

const L = 0.2104542553 * l_ + 0.7936177850 * m_ - 0.0040720468 * s_;
const a = 1.9779984951 * l_ - 2.4285922050 * m_ + 0.4505937099 * s_;
const bb = 0.0259040371 * l_ + 0.7827717662 * m_ - 0.8086757660 * s_;

const C = Math.hypot(a, bb);
const H = (Math.atan2(bb, a) * 180) / Math.PI;

Two things that only show up when you build the inverse:

  • Round trips leave the gamut. OKLCH can express colours sRGB cannot, so converting back produces components outside [0, 1]. Clamping each channel shifts the hue; reducing chroma at constant lightness is the honest fix, and the UI needs to say when it happened.
  • Contrast is not computed on the hex. WCAG's ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) over relative luminance, which is the linear-light value weighted 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. Skipping the linearisation is the classic bug: it passes pairs that fail AA in a real browser. And if a colour has alpha, composite it over the background first.

Cron: the next run time is not "now plus five minutes"

Explaining */15 9-17 * * 1-5 in English is easy. Producing the next six run times is where implementations diverge, because:

  • day-of-month and day-of-week combine with OR, not AND, when both are restricted;
  • 0 and 7 are both Sunday;
  • February 30th has to be skipped, not incremented;
  • a DST jump can make a wall-clock time not exist, or exist twice.

Iterating minute by minute for up to a year is 525,600 checks — fine for one expression, wasteful for six results. Iterating the sets (month → day → hour → minute) is both faster and easier to keep correct. Showing the answer in local time and UTC is the cheapest way to defuse "but it runs at 3am".

Try it on the cron parser.

Diff: trim first, then spend the budget

A textbook LCS table for two 5,000-line files is 25 million cells. Before any of that, trim the common prefix and suffix — on a config diff, that's usually 90% of the file:

let start = 0;
while (start < a.length && start < b.length && a[start] === b[start]) start++;
let endA = a.length - 1, endB = b.length - 1;
while (endA >= start && endB >= start && a[endA] === b[endB]) { endA--; endB--; }

What remains is the actual edit region, where the LCS table is small. When it isn't, the choices are Myers' O(ND) algorithm (fast when the change is small, quadratic when it isn't) or anchoring on unique lines first, as patience diff does. The diff tool also ignores whitespace on request, which is the single most useful option in code review.

JSON → TypeScript, with optionality

Inferring interfaces is a recursion with a merge step. The interesting part is what to do with arrays of objects that differ:

type Shape =
  | { kind: 'object'; props: Map<string, Shape>; seen: number }
  | { kind: 'array'; item: Shape }
  | { kind: 'scalar'; ts: string };

Merge each object into the accumulator, count how many elements contained each key, and mark a key optional when it appears in fewer than all of them. null becomes | null, numbers stay number (unless the literal set is small and closed), and keys that aren't valid identifiers get quoted. The JSON formatter emits the result with nested interfaces named from the path, because Data, Data2, Data3 is what makes generated types useless.

cURL → code is a shell problem, not an HTTP one

Half of that tool is tokenising: \ line continuations, 'single quoted' vs "double quoted $VAR", -H 'A: b' vs -H'A: b'. Only then do you map flags — -X, --data-raw, --data-urlencode, -u, --cookie, -F, --compressed — and emit fetch, Python requests, or Go net/http. Getting --data-urlencode wrong turns a form body into a JSON body and the generated snippet silently fails, which is exactly the bug people use such a tool to avoid.

The UI details that decide whether the tab stays open

  • Run on input, debounced. 120 ms feels instant and keeps typing smooth; a "Run" button feels like 1998 and hides the feedback loop.
  • Errors carry a position. Unexpected token } in JSON at position 42 is useless without underlining character 42.
  • State in the URL hash. #json?input=… makes a result shareable and survives a reload; keep it out of server logs, which the hash does by construction.
  • No layout shift. Reserve the output pane's height before the first result; jumping content is what makes a tool feel broken.
  • Contrast in the UI itself. A contrast checker with unreadable labels is a bad joke, and dark mode needs its own pass.

What the platform still doesn't do for you

navigator.clipboard.writeText needs a secure context and a user gesture; anything else falls back to a hidden textarea and document.execCommand('copy'). Downloads are a Blob plus URL.createObjectURL, and you must revokeObjectURL or leak the file for the life of the tab. And "no server" means no history and no sync — localStorage is the only memory you get, so treat it as a convenience, never as storage.

Fifteen tools later, the thing I'd tell someone starting the same project: the browser gives you more than you think (crypto, URL, Intl, structured clone, workers) and less than you hope (no MD5, no timing-safe compare, no diff, no colour science). Both halves are small, and neither needs a dependency.

The tools are at ryuslog.com/tools; longer write-ups on the same site go deeper on the specifics, for example resource requests, limits and OOMKilled and useEffect dependencies and race conditions.

articles.title: Don't Rewrite Your Ext JS App: Replace It One React Screen at a Time
articles.description: Every few years someone proposes rewriting the old Ext JS front end from scratch. The pitch is always...
articles.body_html:
Every few years someone proposes rewriting the old Ext JS front end from scratch. The pitch is always attractive: a modern stack, a clean design system, no more legacy code. And the result is usually the same: the rewrite takes far longer than planned, the old app keeps getting urgent changes in the meantime, and the business ends up maintaining two systems.

I work on an enterprise application with a large Ext JS front end used by pension administrators every day. We are replacing it with React, but not with a rewrite. We are doing it one screen at a time, with React and Ext JS running side by side in the same application. This post explains why I think that is the right call for most teams, and the practical pattern that makes it work.

Why I don't recommend the big rewrite

Ext JS applications tend to share a few traits:

  • They are big. Grids, forms, wizards and reports built up over many years.
  • They encode business rules nobody wrote down. A field that disables itself in one edge case is often the only record of a regulation or a decision made a decade ago.
  • They are used all day by people who know them deeply. Power users rely on keyboard flows and grid behaviour that a new UI can easily break.

A full rewrite has to rediscover all of that before it delivers anything. Until the very end, users get no benefit, and the team gets no feedback.

Incremental replacement flips that. Every new React screen ships on its own, gets used by real people, and teaches you something before you build the next one.

The pattern: let Ext JS host React components

The core idea is simple. Ext JS stays in charge of the application shell: the layout, the navigation and the existing screens. When we build a new screen, or rebuild an old one, we write it in React and mount it inside an Ext JS component.

Here is a minimal host component, using Ext JS's classic toolkit and React 18. It assumes React and ReactDOM are available to the page, for example from your bundle:

// ReactHost.js
Ext.define('App.view.ReactHost', {
    extend: 'Ext.Component',
    xtype: 'reacthost',

    config: {
        reactComponent: null, // the React component to render
        reactProps: null      // props to pass to it
    },

    afterRender: function () {
        this.callParent(arguments);
        this.root = ReactDOM.createRoot(this.getEl().dom);
        this.renderReact();
    },

    renderReact: function () {
        if (this.root) {
            this.root.render(
                React.createElement(this.getReactComponent(), this.getReactProps() || {})
            );
        }
    },

    updateReactProps: function () {
        // re-render when Ext JS code changes the props
        this.renderReact();
    },

    onDestroy: function () {
        if (this.root) {
            this.root.unmount();
            this.root = null;
        }
        this.callParent(arguments);
    }
});

Using it from an existing Ext JS view looks like any other component:

{
    xtype: 'reacthost',
    reactComponent: NominationSummary,
    reactProps: { memberId: 1042 }
}

Three details matter more than they look:

  1. Mount in afterRender, when the DOM element actually exists.
  2. Always unmount in onDestroy. Ext JS destroys components when tabs and windows close. If React is not unmounted, you leak memory and event listeners, and the bug only shows up after hours of use.
  3. Treat props as the only input. When Ext JS needs to change what React shows, it sets new props through the host. React never reaches into Ext JS components directly.

How the two sides talk to each other

Data flowing into React is handled by props. The harder question is how React tells the rest of the application that something happened, for example "the user saved a record, refresh the grid".

Options, from simplest to most structured:

  • Callback props. The host passes a function such as onSaved in reactProps, and the Ext JS view handles it. This is the easiest place to start.
  • DOM custom events. React dispatches a CustomEvent on its root element and Ext JS listens for it. This is useful when the React component should not know who is listening.
  • A shared API layer. Both sides call the same REST endpoints, and after a change the Ext JS store simply reloads. This keeps the two UIs loosely coupled, which is what you want during a long migration.

What I would avoid is sharing mutable state objects between the two frameworks. Ext JS stores and React state have different update models, and keeping them in sync by hand leads to bugs that are hard to reproduce.

Styling without fights

Ext JS ships with heavy global CSS, and it will happily style elements inside your React component. A few habits keep things predictable:

  • Scope React styles with CSS Modules or a single wrapping class on the React root.
  • Do not rely on CSS resets inside the host. Ext JS already sets many base styles.
  • Match the existing theme at first. Users accept a new screen more easily when it looks like it belongs. You can introduce the new design gradually once more of the app is in React.

Which screens to move first

Not every screen is a good first candidate. Good early choices are:

  • New features, since there is nothing to rewrite, only something to build.
  • Read-heavy summary or review screens, where React's rendering model shines and the risk is low.
  • Screens that are already painful to change in Ext JS, because the team feels the benefit immediately.

Leave the most complex data-entry grids and wizards for later, when the team has a shared React component library and a well-tested integration pattern.

Signs the approach is working

You will know incremental migration is on track when:

  • New features are routinely built in React with no special effort.
  • The host component and integration patterns have stopped changing.
  • Removing an old Ext JS screen is a small, boring pull request.

At that point the balance has shifted, and the remaining Ext JS code can be retired screen by screen until the shell itself is the last thing left.

Final thoughts

Legacy front ends are rarely bad because of the framework. They are hard because they hold years of business knowledge. Incremental migration respects that: it lets you modernise while users keep working, and it turns a risky, all-or-nothing project into a steady series of small wins.

If you are maintaining an Ext JS application and weighing a rewrite, I would love to hear how you are approaching it.

I'm Mackrine Awino, a full-stack software engineer in Nairobi working with Java, Jakarta EE, Spring Boot and React. You can find me on LinkedIn and GitHub.

articles.title: I make 60-second CS explainer videos with no video editor: one HTML file, headless Chrome and ffmpeg
articles.description: I run csip12.in, a small free study site for CBSE Class 11 and 12 Computer Science students in India....
articles.body_html:
I run csip12.in, a small free study site for CBSE Class 11 and 12 Computer Science students in India. Students asked for short videos, so this month I started making 60-second explainers for topics like circuit switching and packet switching.

I do not own a video editor and I did not want to learn one. Instead, each video is a web page that knows how to draw any moment of itself, and a script that takes 30 photos of it per second. Here is how it works and what went wrong along the way.

1. The video is a pure function of time

The whole video is one HTML file at 1080×1920. It has a fixed layout (title, a speech-bubble caption, an SVG area for the animation, progress dots) and one important function:

function render(t) {
  let k = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < DUR.length; i++) if (t >= START[i]) k = i;  // which scene
  const lt = t - START[k];                                          // time inside it
  art.innerHTML = SCENES[k](lt, DUR[k]);                            // SVG string
  cap.innerHTML = CAPTIONS[k];
}

Each scene is a function (localTime, duration) => svgString. There is no requestAnimationFrame, no CSS transitions, no state carried from one frame to the next. Every frame is computed from t alone.

That one rule is what makes the rest easy. I can jump to second 37.4 and see exactly what that frame will look like. I can render frames out of order, or render one still per scene to check the layout before spending ten minutes on a full capture.

The animations are just small helpers on top of that:

const clamp = (x, a = 0, b = 1) => Math.min(b, Math.max(a, x));
const ease  = x => x < .5 ? 2*x*x : 1 - (-2*x + 2)**2 / 2;
// pop(lt, at): 0 before `at`, then a quick overshoot up to 1

A packet moving from router R1 to R2 is lerp(x1, x2, ease(clamp((lt - 1.2) / 0.8))). A label appearing at 2.5 s is scale = pop(lt, 2.5). Once you have five or six of these, building a scene goes surprisingly fast.

2. Taking the photos

A Python script starts Chrome headless with --remote-debugging-port, opens the page over the DevTools protocol, and then loops:

for i in range(int(TOTAL * FPS)):
    await call('Runtime.evaluate', expression=f'render({i / FPS})')
    shot = await call('Page.captureScreenshot', format='jpeg', quality=92)
    save(f'frames/f{i:05d}.jpg', shot['data'])

Two details mattered:

  • Fonts. Before the first frame, I wait on document.fonts.ready and print which font families actually loaded. A fallback font in frame 1 and the real font in frame 40 looks like a glitch.
  • Window size. Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride with 1080×1920 and deviceScaleFactor: 1, so the screenshot is exactly one video frame with no scaling.

A 60-second video is 1,800 screenshots. On my laptop that takes a few minutes, which is fine.

3. Timing comes from the voice, not the other way round

I write the narration first, one line per scene, and generate each line with a text-to-speech model running locally. Then the build script:

  1. trims the silence at both ends of every line with ffmpeg's silenceremove (run forwards, reversed, and forwards again so it trims the end too),
  2. measures each trimmed clip with ffprobe,
  3. sets each scene's duration to the line's length plus 0.85 s of breathing room,
  4. writes those durations into a copy of the HTML file before capturing.

So if I rewrite a sentence and it gets longer, the scene simply gets longer. Nothing needs to be re-timed by hand.

The audio is one ffmpeg -filter_complex: each voice line is delayed to its scene start with adelay, everything is mixed with amix, a quiet background track is added at 8% volume, and loudnorm=I=-14 brings the result to the loudness that YouTube and Facebook expect. The background music is also generated, a four-chord loop of sine waves written with NumPy, so there is nothing to license.

4. Things that bit me

Stale frames. I once shortened a video and the output came out longer than before. The capture had written frames 0–1,850 into a folder that still held frames up to 1,950 from the previous, longer render, and ffmpeg's f%05d.jpg input happily used all of them. The build now deletes the frames folder before every capture.

Checking audio quality without listening to all of it. Local TTS on a 4 GB GPU sometimes returns a take that is just a hum or hiss. Instead of listening to every take, I render a tiny spectrogram for each line (showspectrumpic, 0–4 kHz). Real speech shows clear stacked harmonic stripes, and a bad take shows flat horizontal bars or uniform noise. I glance at ten small images and re-generate only the bad lines.

ffmpeg crashing on contact sheets. I wanted a grid of one still per scene to review layouts at a glance. hstack/xstack with a dozen inputs crashed ffmpeg on Windows with a heap error, so I tile the stills with Pillow instead. It is five lines of code and has never failed.

Text overflow. SVG text does not wrap and does not complain. A table cell like "Store & forward" at font size 38 quietly ran over its box. The only reliable check was the contact sheet: render the stills and look.

Why not just use a video editor?

For one video, an editor is faster. For a series, this approach wins: every video shares the same layout and helpers, so a new topic means writing about ten scene functions and ten sentences. Changing the brand colour or the caption font across all videos is a single line of CSS. And because the video lives in plain text files, I can keep old versions and see exactly what changed between them.

The first one, on circuit switching, is here: Circuit Switching in 60 seconds. The notes it is based on are on csip12.in, and I would be glad to hear from anyone who has built something similar, especially about speeding up the capture loop.

articles.title: Connecting Web Interfaces to AI APIs: A Practical PHP & JavaScript Approach.
articles.description: Integrating AI models into a custom web application doesn't always require a heavy, over-engineered...
articles.body_html:
Integrating AI models into a custom web application doesn't always require a heavy, over-engineered stack. Sometimes, the cleanest way to ship a fast, responsive AI tool is by pairing a lightweight HTML/CSS/JS frontend with a straightforward PHP backend acting as a secure API proxy.

Here is a look at the architecture I use when building custom AI web interfaces under CyberNova, along with a few common pitfalls to watch out for.

Why Use PHP as an API Proxy?
If you call an external AI API (like Groq or Gemini) directly from your frontend JavaScript (fetch), your API key is completely exposed in the browser's Network tab. Routing the request through a local or server-side api.php handler solves two problems at once:

Security: Your API keys stay hidden on the server side.

Control: You can sanitize user inputs, format system prompts, and handle rate limits before hitting the external AI endpoint.

The Request Lifecycle
Frontend (app.js): Captures the user's message, updates the UI optimistically, and sends an asynchronous POST request with JSON data to api.php.

Backend (api.php): Reads the incoming JSON payload (file_get_contents('php://input')), attaches the authorization headers, and forwards the prompt via PHP cURL.

Response Handling: Parses the AI provider's JSON response and sends clean text back to the frontend.

Common Localhost Gotchas (and How to Fix Them)
When testing this setup locally on Windows (using XAMPP/Apache), two issues frequently trip developers up:

SSL Certificate Errors in cURL: Local environments often lack updated CA certificate bundles, causing cURL requests to fail silently or throw gateway errors. While testing locally, setting CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER to false (or properly configuring cacert.pem in php.ini) resolves the handshake issue.

502 Bad Gateway / Timeout Errors: Always set proper CURLOPT_TIMEOUT limits and check curl_error($ch) so your backend returns a clear JSON error message instead of crashing silently.

Wrapping Up
Keeping the stack simple lets you focus on what actually matters: user experience, prompt engineering, and shipping functional tools quickly.

You can check out more of my web and AI work at my CyberNova Portfolio.

How do you prefer handling your AI API proxies—lightweight PHP/Python scripts, or full backend frameworks? Let’s talk in the comments!
